the capture stream buffer under in.lock, ensuring that no stale buffer
pointer can be accessed by submit_audio_out_urb().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: validate the data area in SMB2_read()

SMB2_read() copies le32_to_cpu(rsp->DataLength) bytes from
(char *)rsp + rsp->DataOffset without checking that the range lies
within the response actually received. A READ response with
DataOffset == 0 makes smb2_get_data_area_len() zero the data length, so
smb2_check_message() accepts a frame as short as the fixed response,
while SMB2_read() still uses the server-supplied DataLength, capped only
by CIFS_MAX_MSGSIZE and the caller's length.

A malicious server can answer the synchronous read used by the
mfsymlinks (or SFU) symlink parser with an 81-byte READ response
carrying DataOffset 0 and DataLength 1067, making the client copy 1067
bytes from a 448-byte receive object (KASAN slab-out-of-bounds; up to
16 KiB in the general case).

Clamp a zero (or header-overlapping) DataOffset to read_rsp_size, as
handle_read_data() does for the asynchronous path, and reject the
response unless DataOffset + DataLength fits within rsp_iov.iov_len.
The SMB1 helper was fixed the same way in 5be5bdda5863.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: reserve space for the UTF-16 terminator in stream info

smb_strtoUTF16() always writes a terminating zero UTF-16 unit after the
converted characters, but get_file_stream_info() budgets only
sizeof(struct smb2_file_stream_info) + streamlen * 2 for a stream entry
and sizeof(struct smb2_file_stream_info) + 7 * 2 for the trailing
"::$DATA" entry. When an entry exactly fills the 448-byte small response
buffer, the terminator is written two bytes past the allocation.

Reserve one extra UTF-16 unit in both budget checks. The terminator is
not part of the wire format, so the reported lengths are unchanged.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: fix fiemap wild read on empty truncated response

smb3_fiemap() treats -E2BIG from SMB2_ioctl() as a truncated range blob
and loops for the next chunk. If the server reports
STATUS_BUFFER_OVERFLOW with OutputCount == 0, SMB2_ioctl() returns
-E2BIG with out_data == NULL and out_data_len == 0, and the existing
length checks accept the empty result. The loop then evaluates

	next = out_data[num - 1].file_offset + ...

with num == 0, reading 16 bytes before NULL.

Reject a truncated range blob that contains no range, so the resume
offset is never computed from an empty response. Also require the last
range in a truncated blob to advance the resume offset without
overflowing, and to stay within the requested range; a malicious or
broken server could otherwise make no progress or underflow len and loop
forever. Free the previous response buffer before retrying.

Reproduced on 6.6.87.2 with a malicious SMB2 server that answers
FSCTL_QUERY_ALLOCATED_RANGES with STATUS_BUFFER_OVERFLOW and
OutputCount == 0; an FS_IOC_FIEMAP ioctl on the mount oopses in
cifs_fiemap() with CR2 = fffffffffffffff8. The code path is unchanged
on mainline.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: reject short SESSION_SETUP responses

smb2_check_message() accepts frames shorter than struct smb2_pdu when
the SMB2 status is non-zero, before the minimum-PDU check added by
b4694f269e66d. A 64-byte STATUS_MORE_PROCESSING_REQUIRED SESSION_SETUP
response is therefore accepted even though it cannot contain the
SecurityBufferOffset and SecurityBufferLength fields.

The parser then reads those fields from stale bytes left in the reused
receive buffer by an earlier frame. With a long stale
SecurityBufferLength, decode_ntlmssp_challenge() copies up to about
64 KB from beyond the receive object and sends the data back to the
server in the NTLMv2 AUTHENTICATE target info.

Reject short MPR SESSION_SETUP responses before the short-error path,
and validate SecurityBufferOffset + SecurityBufferLength against the
received response length before decoding the challenge.

The ordering bypass is not new: the short-error early return predates
b4694f269e66d, and the unvalidated SecurityBufferLength read predates
the 2016 raw NTLMSSP split in 166cea4dc3a4, so all supported stable
trees are affected. Reproduced on 6.6.87.2; the path is unchanged on
mainline.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: defer connection scavenging while session locks are busy

The expiration worker holds conn_list_lock for reading while checking
for authenticated sessions. Without this change, the check can wait for
conn->session_lock or sessions_table_lock.

In destroy_previous_session(), the status updates after
ksmbd_conn_wait_idle_sess() run with both session locks held for
writing. Both the KSMBD_SESS_GOOD error path and the
KSMBD_SESS_NEED_SETUP success path call ksmbd_all_conn_set_status(),
which takes conn_list_lock for reading.

A writer queued on conn_list_lock can block these new read acquisitions.
The worker then waits for a session lock held by
destroy_previous_session(), which waits behind the writer. The writer
cannot proceed until the worker releases conn_list_lock.

Try both session locks instead of waiting in the scavenging check. Keep
the connection when either lock is busy and let the periodic worker
retry later.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: hold a connection reference for each session channel

ksmbd_session_unregister() removes a session from the global and per-
connection tables before dropping the table reference. A concurrent
reference holder can keep the session and its channel list alive after
those removals.

Connection cleanup can no longer find the unpublished session to remove its
channels. Since a channel only stores a raw conn pointer, the connection
can be freed while another session reference holder is still accessing it,
for example during SMB3.1.1 binding or a procfs read.

Take a connection reference when registering a channel and release it on
insertion failure, channel removal, or final session destruction. Keep the
channels and signing keys until the session is destroyed so a response can
still be signed after the session has been unregistered.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: limit sessions on each connection

The pending setup limit only counts InProgress sessions. A client can
complete authentication repeatedly and retain an unbounded number of Valid
sessions on one connection.

Reserve a connection slot before allocating a session and retain a
connection reference while authentication is in progress. The first SMB3
channel takes over that reservation; binding to another connection reserves
one slot there. Reauthentication and authentication continuation reuse the
existing reservation. Return slots on allocation or insertion failure,
channel removal, and final session destruction.

Accept max_sessions_per_connection in reserved startup-request space and
default to 64 when older tools leave it zero. Keep the request size and
existing field offsets unchanged. Expose the configured limit in procfs.
The existing connection limits bound the aggregate number of sessions
without a separate global session allocation limit.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: reclaim ended sessions on logoff and expiration

LOGOFF and previous-session replacement leave sessions Expired with a
zero credential expiry. Ended sessions can retain their memory and
connection slots when no further setup arrives on the owning connection.

Unpublish a logged-off session while the request reference keeps its
response signing and encryption keys alive. Remove its procfs entry
before dropping the table reference so a reader cannot remove its own
entry on the last put. Clear proc_entry after removal to avoid removing
it twice.

Reclaim ended sessions from the global table in the existing expiration
worker before it acquires conn_list_lock. Only select Expired sessions
with zero credential expiry and no references beyond the table
reference. Keep sessions whose Kerberos credentials expired available
for reauthentication.

Unlink the session from its setup connection and all channel
connections, so SMB2 sessions and sessions with only secondary SMB3
channels are covered. The session already holds connection references,
and sessions_table_lock prevents concurrent channel removal. Queue
sessions on a separate disposal list, leaving their hash nodes unhashed,
and remove procfs entries and drop table references outside the locks.

Keep the pending setup check before allocating a new session so
abandoned InProgress sessions can release their slots even at the
connection limit. Retain the timeout and reference checks and dispose of
those sessions outside the locks. Leave ended Expired sessions to the
expiration worker.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: drain session procfs readers before dropping table references

Session registration failure and connection cleanup can drop the table
reference while the per-session procfs entry is still accessible. If a
reader holds the last remaining reference, its final put calls
proc_remove() from its own callback and waits for that callback to
finish.

Remove the procfs entry before dropping the table reference in the
registration failure path. Queue sessions removed during connection
cleanup and drain their procfs readers after releasing both session
locks, then return their table references. Keep the global hash node
unhashed while a session is queued so a concurrent unregister cannot
drop the reference again.

Previous-session replacement also destroys the file table before the
session is finally freed. Detach the idr under the lock used by procfs
file counters, and report zero files after it has been detached. This
prevents a reader from accessing the idr during or after its
destruction.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tun: Require CAP_NET_ADMIN to attach to an ownerless device

Twenty years ago I made creating a tuntap device require CAP_NET_ADMIN
in commit ca6bb5d7ab22 ("[NET]: Require CAP_NET_ADMIN to create tuntap
devices.")

The idea was to allow the permissions on /dev/net/tun to be relaxed to
0666 and thus allow owners of tun devices assigned with TUNSETOWNER to
actually open it and get at their devices.

What we missed at the time was that persistent devices with *no* owner
were already essentially world-consumable, and anyone who could open
the device node could also attach to those.

Even then, using persistent devices with no explicitly set owner — on
the (false) presumption that CAP_NET_ADMIN would be required to open
them — wasn't an egregious userspace bug. There are cases where it does
make sense to separate the creation/configuration of the netdevice, from
the process which shovels packets into it.

Since then, TUNSETGROUP was added a year later in commit 8c644623fe7e
("[NET]: Allow group ownership of TUN/TAP devices."). Its commit message
noted that if both uid and gid are set, both have to match (in itself a
bizarre choice) — but still not that with *neither* set, no permission
at all was required.

Then in 2012 commit c8d68e6be1c3 ("tuntap: multiqueue support") allowed
new queues to be attached to a device from the moment of its creation,
with no way for userspace to close the race between creation and a
subsequent TUNSET{OWNER,GROUP}.

In 2024, commit 3ca459eaba1bf ("tun: fix group permission check") tried
to fix things to be saner: only require the user *or* the group to
match, in line with standard POSIX permissions, and require
CAP_NET_ADMIN if neither the user nor group authorised the access
(although it put the CAP_NET_ADMIN check first, and would wrongly have
reported the capability as having been used even when it was not).

That fix was reverted in commit a70c7b3cbc06 ("tun: revert fix group
permission check") due to allegedly causing a regression in an selinux
test suite which *expected* the attachment to succeed when authorised
by none of user, group, nor CAP_NET_ADMIN:
https://lore.kernel.org/netdev/CAFqZXNtkCBT4f+PwyVRmQGoT3p1eVa01fCG_aNtpt6dakXncUg@mail.gmail.com/

We should not break UAPI. But we don't have to consider an selinux test
case which deliberately exercises a security flaw to be UAPI worth
preserving either. To which end, I have fixed it in selinux-testsuite
commit b2f894f0016b ("tests/tun_tap: set an owner on the device for the
relabel tests").

So: fix the lack of CAP_NET_ADMIN check on devices which *haven't* been
assigned an owner or group, while leaving the weird tun ownership model
as it was (user *and* group have to match, if both are set). If someone
still wants to fix the latter (which wasn't actually the reason the
previous attempt was reverted), they can do it under separate cover.

Permit attaching to an existing device only if an owner and/or group was
set and the caller matches all that were set, or if the caller has
CAP_NET_ADMIN. The only behavioural change is that a device with no
owner or group now requires CAP_NET_ADMIN to attach — precisely the
loophole we want to close.

And put the CAP_NET_ADMIN check in the right place this time.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/sched: sch_teql: fix use-after-free on lower qdisc drop

The issue: teql_master_xmit() tests the slave's ndo_start_xmit() return
value against NETDEV_TX_OK alone. A slave that consumes the skb but
returns an error code (rc < NET_XMIT_MASK, e.g. NET_XMIT_DROP) is treated
as if the skb were still owned, so the loop restores skb->dev and calls
__skb_pull() on it. A VLAN slave returns the result of dev_queue_xmit()
from its ndo_start_xmit() (propagated since cbbef5e18307), and when the
lower qdisc drops the packet that value is NET_XMIT_DROP after the skb
has been freed, giving a use-after-free in teql_master_xmit().

The Fix: test for consumption with dev_xmit_complete(), which accepts
NETDEV_TX_OK and every rc < NET_XMIT_MASK, matching other callers that
need to distinguish consumed results from busy. Only NETDEV_TX_OK keeps
the packet counted in tx_packets/tx_bytes and advances the slave; a
consumed result that is neither a success nor NET_XMIT_CN ends the
attempt and is charged to tx_dropped, so lower-qdisc drops are no longer
reported as good transmits. NET_XMIT_CN is counted like success because
it can accompany acceptance of the current packet: pfifo_head_drop drops
the old head, enqueues the current skb and returns NET_XMIT_CN.

Conditions to recreate the bug:
With CONFIG_NET_SCH_TEQL,
CONFIG_VLAN_8021Q and CONFIG_DUMMY enabled, add lkrdummy0 (dummy) and
lkrvlan0 (VLAN id 37 on lkrdummy0); set a pfifo limit 0 root on lkrdummy0
and a teql0 root on lkrvlan0; bring teql0 up with an address and send one
UDP packet to it. The VLAN xmit returns NET_XMIT_DROP from the lower
qdisc while holding a freed skb.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

netfilter: conntrack: tcp: use UNACK timeout for non-closing RST packets

Commit be0502a3f2e9 ("netfilter: conntrack: tcp: only close if RST
matches exact sequence") keeps an established conntrack entry in
ESTABLISHED when an in-window RST does not match the expected sequence
number exactly, so the endpoint can validate the RST with a challenge
ACK.

The timeout selection nevertheless uses the CLOSE timeout for every RST
packet.  The bug is that timeout selection is based on the packet type,
not on the state transition result: even when RST validation keeps
new_state in ESTABLISHED, the timeout is still forced to
TCP_CONNTRACK_CLOSE.

Linux TCP independently rate limits challenge ACKs per socket.  A second
non-exact RST can therefore arrive after the first challenge ACK has
restored the timeout but before the rate limit expires.  The second RST
lowers the timeout to 10 seconds again while the endpoint suppresses the
second challenge ACK, allowing the conntrack entry to expire while both
TCP endpoints remain established.

Using the ESTABLISHED timeout for such RSTs would avoid this short
expiration window, but it could also retain stale entries for the
five-day default because conntrack cannot reliably match the endpoint's
exact TCP state.

Use the UNACK timeout for RST packets that leave the conntrack entry in
TCP_CONNTRACK_ESTABLISHED.  Exact-match RSTs and accepted RST packet
trains still fall through to timeouts[new_state], which preserves the
CLOSE timeout when conntrack accepts the RST as closing the flow.

This avoids the aggressive 10-second expiration window for non-exact
RSTs while preserving the short timeout for RSTs that conntrack accepts
as closing the flow.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: skbuff: propagate shared-frag marker in skb_zerocopy()

skb_zerocopy() moves frag descriptors from @from into @to and takes a
reference on each frag, but it does not copy skb_shinfo(from)->flags into
skb_shinfo(to)->flags.  A destination skb holding the same page-cache
backed frags as the source therefore reports skb_has_shared_frag() as
false.

That breaks the invariant relied on by later in-place writers.  ESP input
checks skb_has_shared_frag() before deciding whether an uncloned
nonlinear skb can skip skb_cow_data(); with the marker lost, an skb that
skb_zerocopy() built for nfnetlink_queue or for an openvswitch upcall is
decrypted in place, letting an unprivileged user write into the page
cache of a root-owned read-only file.

Propagate SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG when frag descriptors are copied, as done for
the other frag-transfer helpers.

imgproxy 3.3.0 before 4.0.17 contains an out-of-bounds heap read and write in the ICO loader's BMP header reconstruction (vips_foreign_load_ico_header in vips/icoload.c) when an ICO entry declares a tiny data size, causing unvalidated header fields to be read and written past the allocated buffer. Unauthenticated remote attackers can supply a crafted ICO image to corrupt adjacent heap chunk metadata, triggering a glibc abort that crashes the worker.

OpenEMR from 7.0.1 before 8.4.0 contains a flaw in src/Common/Auth/OneTimeAuth.php that ignores the enforce_onetime_use and max_access_count flags, never revokes consumed service_auth tokens, and checks login_pin without rate limiting or strict comparison. Attackers holding a captured token can replay it or brute-force the PIN to open patient-portal sessions exposing PHI.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains a path traversal vulnerability in the FaxSMS module's RCFaxClient and SignalWireClient disposeDocument functions that allows authenticated low-privilege users to read and overwrite arbitrary files via the unsanitized file_path parameter. Attackers can request action=download to retrieve cleartext files like sqlconf.php database credentials and keys, or use action=setup to overwrite web-server-writable files with ciphertext.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains a broken access control and path traversal vulnerability in the fax/sms module disposeDocument action via an unvalidated file_path parameter. Authenticated low-privilege users can read sqlconf.php to recover database credentials and write arbitrary files as the web user, enabling remote code execution.

OpenEMR before 8.4.0 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability in its SMART on FHIR implementation because checkUserHasAccessToPatient() in BearerTokenAuthorizationStrategy.php unconditionally returns true. Authenticated users or malicious SMART apps can manipulate token launch context to bind requests to arbitrary patient UUIDs, gaining unauthorized read/write access to other patients' FHIR resources.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability in interface/forms/eye_mag/report.php that allows authenticated users to inject scripts by adding unescaped document notes. Attackers with document-note write access can store malicious JavaScript in a retina document note that executes when clinicians generate the Eye Exam patient report, exposing session cookies.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains an insecure direct object reference vulnerability in portal/lib/persist.php that allows authenticated portal patients to write settings for other patients. Attackers can modify the setting_patient parameter in a JSON POST request to another patient's PID, altering that patient's portal settings such as the portal theme.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains missing authorization and insecure direct object reference vulnerabilities in the oe-module-prior-authorizations module that allow authenticated low-privilege users to access and modify other patients' records. Attackers can request public/reports/list_report.php to view all patients' names, MRNs, insurance and prior-auth data, or submit arbitrary id values to public/index.php to overwrite other patients' prior-authorization records.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains a path traversal vulnerability in interface/billing/sl_eob_process.php that allows authenticated users to write and read files by supplying unsanitized eraname values. Attackers without billing privileges can inject ../ sequences to create ERA report .html files anywhere the web user can write and parse arbitrary .edi files echoed into the report.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains an insecure direct object reference vulnerability in many encounter-form view and save endpoints that lack patient/encounter ownership checks. Authenticated clinical users can enumerate sequential form id values in requests such as soap/view.php and save.php to read and overwrite other patients' clinical records.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in library/ajax/upload.php that allows any authenticated user to read and overwrite document data by supplying an arbitrary doc_id. Low-privilege users can enumerate doc_id values with the fetch and save actions to disclose patient health information and tamper with medical records across all patients.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability that allows authenticated users with CAMOS access to inject HTML by saving malicious CAMOS content through ajax_save.php. Attackers can store a script payload that executes unencoded when the entry is printed via the non-print_html branch of rx_print.php, performing actions and reading data as the victim user.

OpenEMR before 8.4.0 contains a local file inclusion in the ESign router (library/ESign/Router.php), which passes the unsanitized module parameter into a require_once of '<module>/Controller.php', and the fax module's faxProcessUploads writes attacker-named files to a predictable temp path without extension checks. Authenticated attackers can upload a PHP file named Controller.php, then request interface/esign/index.php with a traversing module parameter to include it and execute arbitrary code.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains a broken object level authorization vulnerability in portal/report/portal_custom_report.php that allows authenticated portal patients to read other patients' problem list entries. Attackers can enumerate sequential IDs in issue_ parameter names to retrieve other patients' problem titles, clinical notes, ICD diagnosis codes, and IPPF contraceptive records.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in interface/billing/sl_eob_invoice.php that allows any authenticated user to read and modify billing data for any encounter. Attackers can iterate the id parameter to read patient names and billing notes, and post payments, adjustments, deletions, or billing notes against any patient's account.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in interface/billing/sl_eob_patient_note.php that allows any authenticated user to read and modify patient billing notes. Attackers with low-privilege accounts can enumerate the patient_id parameter and submit POST requests using the embedded CSRF token to view or tamper with confidential billing data.

MRBS (Meeting Room Booking System) before 1.12.3 contains a reflected cross-site scripting vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to inject script via the error parameter of view_entry.php. Attackers can send crafted links to logged-in users to read CSRF tokens, modify or delete bookings, or perform administrative actions.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains an insecure direct object reference vulnerability in portal/lib/persist.php that allows authenticated portal patients to modify other patients' settings by supplying an arbitrary setting_patient value. Attackers can insert or overwrite patient_settings rows for victims to suppress notifications, tamper with consent flags, or alter portal preferences.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains an insecure direct object reference in portal/lib/paylib.php, which writes the request-supplied form_pid (or the patient_id_cc value in Sphere data) to onsite_portal_activity without checking it against the session patient. Authenticated portal patients can submit portal-save, review-save, AuthorizeNet, Stripe, or Sphere requests to insert or modify forged payment-audit records in other patients' billing records.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains a missing authorization vulnerability that allows low-privileged authenticated users to delete arbitrary patient recall records via the delete_Recall action. Attackers can send POST requests to /interface/main/messages/save.php with a target pid and r_ID to remove recall data without ACL or ownership checks.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the addRecall action of /interface/main/messages/save.php that allows low-privileged authenticated users to modify arbitrary patients' recall data. Attackers can submit a crafted new_pid with recall, contact, provider, facility, and notification preference fields to overwrite records of patients they cannot access.

OpenEMR before 8.4.0 contains an arbitrary local file read vulnerability in REST document download, where the controller passes stored uploaded document bytes to Symfony's BinaryFileResponse as a filesystem path instead of returning them as content. Authenticated users with document upload and download access can upload a document containing an absolute pathname, such as the sqlconf.php location, then download it to read server files and recover database credentials.

OpenEMR before 8.4.0 contains an improper authorization vulnerability in Rainforest patient portal payments that trusts browser-supplied patientId, encounter, and amount values instead of deriving them from the portal session. Authenticated portal patients can tamper with JSON sent to portal_payment.rainforest.php so the payin.authorized webhook writes forged ar_activity credits to other patients' encounters exceeding the amount actually paid.

OpenEMR before 8.4.0 contains an authorization bypass allowing low-privileged SMART standalone-launch users to bind arbitrary patient UUIDs into the OAuth token context. Attackers with only the patients|demo ACL can select a victim during authorization and read that patient's clinical notes and documents through patient-scoped DocumentReference and Binary FHIR endpoints.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability that allows authenticated clinicians lacking high-sensitivity permission to read and modify encounter-bound forms via load_form.php. Attackers can request the Clinical Notes or Care Plan direct loader to obtain restricted content and a CSRF token, then submit save.php to tamper with clinical records.

OpenEMR before 8.3.0 contains a broken access control vulnerability in portal/portal_payment.php that allows low-privilege authenticated users to bypass billing ACL checks by tampering patient identifiers. Attackers can modify the pid and form_pid parameters to view payment pages and record fraudulent payment receipts for arbitrary patients, corrupting billing records.

A flaw has been found in SourceCodester Simple CRUD using PHP and FPDF 1.0. Affected by this vulnerability is an unknown functionality of the file app/register.php. Executing a manipulation of the argument firstname can lead to sql injection. The attack can be executed remotely. The exploit has been published and may be used.

A security flaw has been discovered in iomad up to 4.5.15/5.0.11/5.1.8/5.2.4. Affected by this vulnerability is the function local_iomad_pluginfile in the library public/local/iomad/lib.php of the component PDF Certificate Handler. The manipulation results in authorization bypass. The attack can be launched remotely. The patch is identified as ac7427130865ce0ed80870813317c87ae3060fa4/7bf0b10199782e04aa579e9d516e473b164afd1c/db903abdcb3aba124cce670608ae6d7ba5f51a84/66f7417c5357b7575e39e8be390602156c1a1225. It is advisable to implement a patch to correct this issue. This CVE was requested by the vendor.

rConfig Core 8.0.0 before 8.2.19 and rConfig Pro before 8.4.1 contain a deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability that allows unauthenticated network attackers to execute arbitrary code by pushing a crafted serialized job onto the Redis-backed Laravel Horizon queue, which runs without authentication in affected deployments. Laravel's CallQueuedHandler unserializes the job without class restrictions, allowing attackers to instantiate the existing App\\Jobs\\TaskDownloadRun class and invoke an attacker-controlled Artisan command. Attackers can leverage the bundled laravel/tinker package to execute arbitrary PHP and operating system commands as the queue worker's user, write a persistent web shell into the web-served storage/app/public directory, and read database credentials, stored device credentials, and API tokens. Where Redis is not directly reachable, authenticated attackers can deliver the payload through the application by configuring a device target that points at the rConfig server's loopback address.

A weakness has been identified in PipraPay 3.0.0. Affected by this vulnerability is the function hash_hmac of the file pp-content/pp-include/pp-adapter.php of the component pp-token anti-CSRF Handler. Executing a manipulation can lead to hard-coded credentials. The attack may be performed from remote. The exploit has been made available to the public and could be used for attacks. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

A security vulnerability has been detected in PipraPay 3.0.0. Affected by this issue is the function deleteData of the file pp-content/pp-include/pp-functions.php of the component Admin Panel. The manipulation of the argument selected_ids/ItemID leads to sql injection. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The exploit has been disclosed publicly and may be used. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

compose-lint is a Docker Compose security linter that identifies dangerous misconfigurations before deployment. From 0.22.0 until 0.31.0, compose-lint follows a sibling .env symbolic link outside the project without applying its normal containment check. From 0.28.0, the same gap also affects an include project_directory link outside the project. A pull request can reference a variable from the linked file, causing substitution to place runner file or process-environment data into finding messages written to logs, JSON, SARIF artifacts, and Code Scanning alerts. Reading /proc/self/environ can expose the remainder of the linter process environment because NUL-separated entries are treated as one value, although disclosure requires a workflow that processes untrusted changes with useful environment data and GitHub normally withholds secrets from fork pull requests. The pass or fail result is not changed. This issue is fixed in version 0.31.0.

compose-lint is a Docker Compose security linter that identifies dangerous misconfigurations before deployment. From 0.9.0 until 0.18.0, compose-lint's YAML parser recognizes lone carriage returns and Unicode line separators U+0085, U+2028, and U+2029 as line breaks while fix position conversion counts only newline characters. A pull request can place one of these separators in a quoted value so fix --apply shifts each later edit and deletes the line after the selected target, including an unselected network or other security setting. The resulting Compose file can remain valid, post-edit checks can pass, and the command can report a successful fix even though the dry-run diff was the only place showing the extra deletion. This issue is fixed in version 0.18.0.

compose-lint is a Docker Compose security linter that identifies dangerous misconfigurations before deployment. From 0.22.0 until 0.32.0, compose-lint substitutes values from a sibling .env file into image fields and quotes the resolved value in CL-0004 and CL-0019 finding messages and fix text. In a workflow that writes secrets into that file and then lints untrusted pull-request content, an attacker can reference a secret variable so its whole value reaches the job log, JSON output, SARIF artifacts, and Code Scanning alerts. Fork pull requests normally lack secrets, so exploitation requires a secret-bearing workflow such as pull_request_target, same-repository branches, or a retained .env on a self-hosted runner, and the pass or fail result is unchanged. This issue is fixed in version 0.32.0.

compose-lint is a Docker Compose security linter that identifies dangerous misconfigurations before deployment. From 0.32.0 until 0.33.0, compose-lint's incomplete remediation for .env secret disclosure checks the 20,000-finding limit before replacing resolved values with their variable references. A pull request can combine a secret-referencing image field with aliased content that produces more than 20,000 findings, causing the early-stop path to emit already graded findings with the resolved secret value in text, JSON, SARIF, and Code Scanning output. Exploitation requires a workflow that writes secrets into the sibling .env and lints untrusted changes, and the run exits 2 unless --allow-partial-coverage is used. This issue is fixed in version 0.33.0.

A flaw was found in ansible-core's ansible.builtin.git module. The module
invokes git (ls-remote, clone, fetch) with the repository URL as a positional
argument and without a "--" separator, so a repository URL that begins with a
dash is interpreted by git as a command-line option. A caller that passes an
attacker-controlled repository URL to the module can trigger argument
injection (for example --upload-pack/--exec), resulting in arbitrary command
execution on the host running the module.

A security vulnerability has been detected in iomad up to 4.5.15/5.0.11/5.1.8/5.2.4. Affected by this issue is the function store_temporary_password of the file public/local/iomad/classes/company_user.php of the component Password Field Handler. Such manipulation leads to information disclosure. The attack may be performed from remote. The attack requires a high level of complexity. The exploitation is known to be difficult. The name of the patch is 0d9c0ccaa8a77583f5dd92eb7be7fbbb8cc6ec9b/9c740fd254fd12d56d7be3b85ac5e9fb4f8c03d8/33755cdd551a84be423b1eaf784d405c1988dbad/7fcf9b52c539a67f3e46a8da6b42ab1d1f26295b. It is advisable to implement a patch to correct this issue. This CVE was requested by the vendor.

The OpenSSL library bundled with the Illumio VEN is affected by an uncontrolled search path vulnerability. A low-privileged, authenticated local attacker could potentially leverage this vulnerability to execute arbitrary code with elevated privileges.

pyLoad is a free and open-source download manager written in Python. Prior to 0.5.0b3.dev102, UnTar._safe_extractall in src/pyload/plugins/extractors/UnTar.py validates archive member paths and link targets but does not call TarInfo.isdev to reject special tar member types before calling tarfile.extractall. On supported Python 3.9 through 3.13 runtimes, tarfile defaults to the fully_trusted extraction filter, so a user with ADD and STATUS permissions can cause extraction of a crafted archive containing character devices, block devices, or FIFOs. Python 3.14 defaults to a safe extraction filter. When pyLoad runs with operating-system privileges that permit device creation, including the official root-based Docker deployment, the archive can expose raw devices and compromise the host. Non-root deployments can still create FIFOs that cause hangs or IPC confusion. This issue is fixed in version 0.5.0b3.dev102.

djust provides Phoenix LiveView-style reactive server-side rendering for Django with Rust-powered performance. Prior to versions 1.0.10 and 1.1.2, djust keys context output-safety grants by variable name and fails to revoke a grant when a template bind replaces the value associated with that name. A template using {% with %}, {% for %}, {% include ... with %}, tuple unpacking, or assign tags can therefore rebind a name that previously held mark_safe content and emit the new attacker-controlled value without escaping, including descendant lookups through the rebound name. This can cause stored or reflected cross-site scripting when a victim renders the affected template. This issue is fixed in versions 1.0.10 and 1.1.2.

ModSecurity is an open source, cross platform web application firewall (WAF) engine for Apache, IIS and Nginx. Prior to 2.9.15 and 3.0.17, t:htmlEntityDecode recognizes only a small subset of named HTML entities, so rules that depend on the transformation can inspect different bytes than a browser or backend. Attackers can encode ASCII separators and operators with unhandled entity names, including aliases, to bypass rules that depend on the transformation. The v3 decoder also accepts prefix matches instead of requiring an exact entity-token length, which can transform invalid longer names into different bytes. This issue is fixed in versions 2.9.15 and 3.0.17.

titra is an open source time tracking project. In versions 1.0.3 and prior, authenticated API users can abuse the customfields object to inject or overwrite top-level fields in MongoDB documents. At time of publication, there are no publicly known patches.

Mongoose is a MongoDB object modeling tool designed to work in an asynchronous environment. Prior to 6.13.12, 7.8.13, 8.24.7, and 9.11.4, Mongoose uses attacker-controlled discriminator key values, including the default __t field, to index plain-object registries such as Model.discriminators and schema.discriminators without requiring an own property. Values such as constructor, toString, or hasOwnProperty can therefore resolve to inherited built-in functions instead of a registered discriminator, causing type confusion in model construction, document creation, hydration, query and update casting, embedded discriminators, and populate operations. In the bulkWrite() insertOne path with skipValidation enabled, a constructor value can cause a raw input object to be stored without schema casting or strict filtering, and a stored poisoned document can make every query that hydrates it fail until the document is removed. The weakness reads inherited properties but does not modify Object.prototype and is not prototype pollution. This issue is fixed in versions 6.13.12, 7.8.13, 8.24.7, and 9.11.4.

Mongoose is a MongoDB object modeling tool designed to work in an asynchronous environment. Prior to 6.13.12, 7.8.13, 8.24.7, and 9.11.4, Schema.prototype.virtual() builds nested virtual paths without applying the special-property validation already used by Schema.path() and Schema.add(). An attacker who can influence virtual field names in dynamic schemas, content-management form builders, or schema-as-code systems can supply path segments such as __proto__, constructor, or prototype, causing the virtual-path reducer to write enumerable properties to Object.prototype or Function.prototype. The resulting prototype pollution can spoof inherited property checks such as authorization flags and can provide function-prototype gadget state to other server-side JavaScript code. This issue is fixed in versions 6.13.12, 7.8.13, 8.24.7, and 9.11.4.

Mongoose is a MongoDB object modeling tool designed to work in an asynchronous environment. Prior to 6.13.11, 7.8.12, 8.24.3, and 9.9.2, Mongoose countDocuments() does not apply the configured sanitizeFilter query selector injection defense. An application that enables sanitizeFilter and passes attacker-controlled filter values to countDocuments() can therefore process query operator objects as operators rather than literal values, causing the count to include documents that should not match and potentially undermining authorization or application logic based on that count. This issue is fixed in versions 6.13.11, 7.8.12, 8.24.3, and 9.9.2.

A vulnerability was found in SourceCodester Smart Attendance System with QR Code Scanner 1.0. Affected is an unknown function of the file api/attendance_handler.php of the component JSON Endpoint. Performing a manipulation of the argument student_code results in missing authentication. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The exploit has been made public and could be used.

Tencent BrowserSkill through 0.4.2 contains a missing authentication vulnerability that allows local attackers to impersonate the bsk daemon because remoteSocket() connects to the loopback WebSocket without credentials or peer verification. Attackers who bind the daemon port before it starts or after it exits receive the extension's full tool surface, including evaluate, to run JavaScript through CDP in logged-in browser tabs.

DataRoom through 3.0.0 contains an sql injection vulnerability in MyBatisService.generateSql that allows sharer-role users to inject SQL by supplying crafted dataset parameters. Attackers can send crafted inputParam values to /dataRoom/dataset/run, exploiting unquoted string parameters or MySQL backslash escapes, to execute injected SQL against the database.

Group-Office before 6.8.181, 25.0.116, and 26.0.58 contains an arbitrary local file read vulnerability in FolderController::actionProcessUploadQueue that allows authenticated users to read server files by supplying absolute paths in the blobs parameter. Attackers can have files hard-linked or copied into their own folder and downloaded, exposing other users' stored files and config.php database credentials.

The WPML Multilingual CMS plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass via Race Condition in versions up to, and including, 4.9.7. This is due to the `process_iframe_request` function's language-per-domain SSO handler generating the cross-domain sign-in token via `wp_create_nonce('wpml_sso')` on the logout landing page, where the browser has already discarded its authentication cookies — so `wp_get_session_token()` returns an empty string and the token collapses to the shared anonymous nonce for the current 12-hour tick rather than a user-bound secret — and then storing it in the `wpml_sso_user_<token>_<sha256('wpml_sso'.$domain)>` transient mapped to the victim's `user_id` with no binding to the specific sign-out action or requesting client. Because an unauthenticated attacker can independently derive the identical token by triggering the logout confirmation flow on `wp-login.php?action=logout`, and because the `is_iframe_request()` gate conditions (the per-domain SSO `started` transient and domain-hash derived from the public constant `SSO_NONCE`) are fully computable within the 60-second `SSO_TIMEOUT` window, an unauthenticated attacker can submit the forged `wpml_sso_token_domain` parameter with a `wpml_user_signed_in` status to a secondary language-domain endpoint before the legitimate `wpml_user_signed_out` iframe fires, causing WordPress authentication cookies to be issued for the victim. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to gain access to accounts of users — including administrators — who are actively in the process of logging out during the race window.

A flaw was found in cockpit-storaged. A Tang keyserver address read from a clevis token in a LUKS header is concatenated into curl's argument vector without a "--" separator. An address beginning with "-" is parsed by curl as an option instead of a hostname, allowing an attacker who can attach a crafted LUKS/clevis block device (for example, a local unprivileged user with an active console or desktop login session) to have an administratively-privileged Cockpit user unknowingly trigger curl option injection when editing the device's Tang keyserver settings. This can lead to arbitrary file read or write as the Cockpit session user.
Zoho Corporation ManageEngine DDI Central versions 6200 and below are vulnerable to LDAP bind password exposure through insufficiently protected LDAP settings API.
Zoho Corporation ManageEngine DDI Central version below 6201 is vulnerable to SQL injection in HA replication username handling leading to command execution as the PostgreSQL service account.
Zoho Corporation ManageEngine DDI Central versions 6200 and below are vulnerable to Cisco IOS command injection via DHCP pool name leading to arbitrary commands on managed Cisco routers.

A flaw was found in flightctl. A TLS handshake is performed synchronously in the HTTP server’s connection-context callback without a deadline. A network-reachable unauthenticated client can stall the handshake and prevent the affected listener from accepting new connections.

V programming language standard library net.http through version 0.5.2 prior to commit 4077484 contains a TLS certificate validation bypass vulnerability that allows on-path attackers to intercept HTTPS traffic by exploiting the default false value of SSLConnectConfig.validate and FetchConfig.validate, which completes TLS handshakes without verifying certificates in both the mbedtls and OpenSSL backends. Attackers can present an expired, self-signed, wrong-hostname, or untrusted-root certificate to successfully complete the handshake via http.get, http.post, or http.fetch, enabling interception or modification of HTTPS traffic unless validate: true is explicitly configured.

Docker Desktop before version 4.94.0 could write the signed-in user's Docker Hub access token (a JWT) in cleartext to application logs and diagnostics bundles. IPC payloads that were bare JSON strings or arrays were not redacted before logging, and a Docker Desktop component logged the token when it requested it from the backend. An attacker with read access to these files could obtain the token and use it to read and modify the user's Docker Hub data as that user while the token remains valid. Docker Desktop 4.94.0 redacts these payloads. The fix does not rewrite logs written by earlier versions, which can still contain tokens after upgrading.

After a successful WS-Security UsernameToken authentication, the caller identity stays associated with the worker thread once the request completes when web services are served by the standalone OpenEJB HTTP server. A remote unauthenticated attacker whose request is later processed on the same thread can invoke protected EJB methods with the identity of a previously authenticated user. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 10.3.0 or 11.0.0-M2, which fix the issue.

The embedded OpenEJB HTTP server does not isolate HTTP sessions between web applications. A remote attacker can use a session established in one web application in another one, which then trusts session state set by the first application. Only deployments hosting several web applications on the embedded HTTP server are affected. Users are recommended to block network access to the embedded HTTP server from untrusted clients, or to migrate to the Tomcat based TomEE distributions.

The Jakarta Security identity store backed by the Tomcat user database compares the supplied password with the stored value as plain text and ignores the configured credential handler. When digested passwords are stored, an attacker who obtained a stored digest, for example from a leaked users file or backup, can authenticate with the digest instead of the password. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 10.3.0 or 11.0.0-M2, which fix the issue.

The embedded OpenEJB HTTP server reports every request as authenticated when an application requests authentication programmatically. A remote unauthenticated attacker can access functionality protected this way. Only applications served by the embedded HTTP server that rely on programmatic authentication are affected. Users are recommended to block network access to the embedded HTTP server from untrusted clients, or to migrate to the Tomcat based TomEE distributions.

When JAX-WS or JAX-RS endpoints are published by the embedded OpenEJB HTTP server rather than Tomcat, some configured authentication methods are silently ignored and the endpoint is published without authentication. A remote unauthenticated attacker can invoke the exposed operations without credentials. Only deployments that use the embedded HTTP server and rely on such an authentication method are affected. Users are recommended to block network access to the embedded HTTP server from untrusted clients, or to migrate to the Tomcat based TomEE distributions.

ZenTao PMS through 22.7 contains a missing object-level authorization vulnerability in module/build/control.php that allows authenticated users to modify builds in projects they do not belong to. Attackers holding build privileges in any project can supply sequential buildID values to delete, edit, or relink stories and bugs on builds in foreign or private projects.

Dolibarr 20.0.0 through 23.0.4 and 24.x before 24.0.2 contains an insecure direct object reference vulnerability in api_expensereports.class.php payment endpoints that lets authenticated users access other users' expense report payments. Attackers with only expense report read and create rights can call getAllPayments, getPayments, addPayment, or updatePayment to read, create, or modify payments, falsifying reimbursement state.

The embedded OpenEJB HTTP server does not limit the size of incoming request bodies or of multipart requests, and does not remove the temporary files it creates for multipart parts. A remote unauthenticated attacker can cause excessive memory or disk usage, leading to denial of service. Deployments using the Tomcat connectors are not affected. Users are recommended to block network access to the embedded HTTP server from untrusted clients, or to migrate to the Tomcat based TomEE distributions.

The embedded Derby network service ignores its configured bind address and listens on all network interfaces. When the service is enabled, a remote attacker with network access can connect to the database server and read or modify data. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 10.3.0 or 11.0.0-M2, which fix the issue.

When Hessian remoting endpoints are served by the embedded HTTP server, configured authentication and transport security requirements are silently ignored. A remote unauthenticated attacker can invoke the exposed EJB methods without credentials or over an unencrypted connection. Only deployments that use the embedded HTTP server rather than Tomcat and rely on these settings are affected. Users are recommended to block network access to Hessian endpoints from untrusted clients, or to migrate to another remoting protocol.

The embedded OpenEJB HTTP server dispatches some requests to REST endpoints configured for HTTP Basic authentication without verifying credentials. A remote unauthenticated attacker can invoke protected resources, bypassing authentication. Only deployments that use the embedded HTTP server with Basic authentication are affected. Users are recommended to block network access to the embedded HTTP server from untrusted clients, or to migrate to the Tomcat based TomEE distributions.

The embedded OpenEJB HTTP server does not restrict static resource paths to the configured resource directories. A remote unauthenticated attacker can read arbitrary files accessible to the server process. Users are recommended to block network access to the embedded HTTP server from untrusted clients, or to migrate to the Tomcat based TomEE distributions.

The embedded HTTP server does not clear the security identity established during a request before its worker thread handles the next request. A remote unauthenticated attacker can have their request processed with the identity of a previously authenticated user, gaining that user's privileges. Only applications served by the embedded HTTP server that authenticate programmatically or via basic authentication are affected. Users are recommended to block network access to the embedded HTTP server from untrusted clients, or to migrate to the Tomcat based TomEE distributions.

The embedded HTTP server does not invalidate the previous session identifier when an application changes the session id, e.g. after login. An attacker who can plant a session identifier in a victim's browser can hijack the victim's authenticated session. Users are recommended to block network access to the embedded HTTP server from untrusted clients, or to migrate to the Tomcat based TomEE distributions.

In Eclipse Kura versions 5.4.0 through 5.6.2, the Service Listing V1 REST API read the JSON body of every request into memory, with no limit on its size. The endpoints parse the body before they check whether the caller is authenticated. A remote attacker without valid credentials can therefore send a few dozen large JSON requests at the same time, exhaust the Java heap with an `OutOfMemoryError`, and cause a denial of service. Likewise, a remote attacker, can send a deeply nested JSON request and trigger a `StackOverflowError` because of an unbound recursion in Service Listing V1.

compose-lint is a Docker Compose security linter that identifies dangerous misconfigurations before deployment. In version 0.31.0, compose-lint does not sanitize the ##[ workflow-command opener inside strings written by --format json or --format sarif to stdout. A pull request can place that opener in a service name or other Compose value, and the GitHub Actions runner recognizes it even in the middle of a serialized line when the package, pre-commit hook, or Docker image prints JSON or SARIF to the job log. Writing the output to a file and using the compose-lint GitHub Action are not affected, and the flaw does not change the lint pass or fail result. This issue is fixed in version 0.32.0.

compose-lint is a Docker Compose security linter that identifies dangerous misconfigurations before deployment. In version 0.31.0, compose-lint does not neutralize the Azure Pipelines ##vso[ logging-command opener on any output path. A pull request can place that opener in a Compose value or file name, allowing output from the package, pre-commit hook, or Docker image to issue logging commands when printed to an Azure Pipelines job log. The maintainer did not reproduce the behavior on an Azure Pipelines agent. The GitHub Action is not affected because it runs only on GitHub Actions, and releases before 0.31.0 are outside this advisory because they did not claim Azure Pipelines coverage. This issue is fixed in version 0.32.0.

Group-Office is an enterprise customer relationship management and groupware tool. Prior to version 26.0.37, go/modules/community/bookmarks/controller/Bookmark.php's description() action takes a fully attacker-controlled url parameter and passes it, unvalidated, to \GO\Base\Util\HttpClient::request(). HttpClient::_initRequest() sets CURLOPT_URL directly from this value with no host/IP validation at all. This can result in SSRF via Bookmark/description JMAP action. This issue has been patched in version 26.0.37.

pgEdge Postgres MCP Server enables SQL queries against PostgreSQL databases through Model Context Protocol compatible clients. Prior to 1.1.0, the HTTP transport did not validate the Origin header on incoming requests. A user who visited an attacker-controlled page could be targeted through DNS rebinding, allowing the page to reach a locally running server and read schemas and query results from configured databases. The issue affected deployments with the HTTP transport enabled on a machine that also ran a browser, while the default stdio transport was not reachable through this path. This issue is fixed in version 1.1.0.

pgEdge Postgres MCP Server enables SQL queries against PostgreSQL databases through Model Context Protocol compatible clients. Prior to 1.1.0, the where parameter of the count_rows tool accepted subqueries against tables other than the table named in the tool call. A caller could use predicates and the returned row count as an inference oracle to extract data from any other table that the connected database role could read. The database privilege boundary remained intact, and the flaw did not grant access to tables outside that role's existing SELECT privileges. This issue is fixed in version 1.1.0.

pgEdge RAG Server is an API server for retrieval-augmented generation over PostgreSQL content using pgvector. Prior to 2.0.0, the BM25 keyword index is a single per-pipeline object shared by the unauthenticated query endpoint, and concurrent requests lock its clear, refill, and search operations separately. This allows one request to search a corpus populated through another request's search filter, which can return documents belonging to a different tenant or customer without malformed input. The affected responses cannot be identified retrospectively from the server logs. This issue is fixed in version 2.0.0.

NocoBase is an AI-powered no-code/low-code platform for building business applications and enterprise solutions. Versions 2.1.0 through 2.1.14 contain a server-side request forgery vulnerability in the customRequests:send endpoint. A low-privileged authenticated user can override the stored request URL at runtime using options.url, causing the NocoBase server to send requests to attacker-controlled or internal destinations. Exploitation could expose internal services, Docker host gateways, or cloud metadata endpoints and allow the server to be used as a trusted network proxy. This issue has been fixed in version 2.1.15.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

netfilter: nft_byteorder: remove multi-register support

64bit byteorder conversion is broken when several registers need to be
converted because the source register array advances in steps for 4 bytes
instead of 8:

  for (i = ...
      src64 = nft_reg_load64(&src[i]);
                             ~~~~~ u32 *src
      nft_reg_store64(&dst64[i],

Remove the multi-register support, it has other issues as well:

Pablo points out that commit
caf3ef7468f7 ("netfilter: nf_tables: prevent OOB access in nft_byteorder_eval")
alters semantics: before the loop operated on registers, i.e.
 for ( ... )
   dst32[i] = htons((u16)src32[i])

 .. but after the patch it will operate on bytes, which makes this
 useless to convert e.g. concatenations, which store each compound
 in its own register.

Multi-convert of u32 has one theoretical application:

ct mark . meta mark . tcp dport @intervalset

Because ct mark and meta mark are host byte order, use with
intervals has to convert the byteorder for ct/meta mark value
to network byte order (bigendian).

nftables emits this:
 [ meta load mark => reg 1 ]
 [ byteorder reg 1 = hton(reg 1, 4, 4) ]
 [ ct load mark => reg 9 ]
 [ byteorder reg 9 = hton(reg 9, 4, 4) ]
 ...

I.e. two separate calls.  Theoretically it could be changed to do:
 [ meta load mark => reg 1 ]
 [ ct load mark => reg 9 ]
 [ byteorder reg 1 = htonl(reg 1, 4, 8) ]
 ...

But then all it would take to change the set to
meta mark . tcp dport . ct mark

... and we'd be back to two "byteorder" calls. IOW, support to
convert a range of registers is both dysfunctional and dubious.

Simplify this: remove the feature.

Pablo Neira Ayuso points out that nftables before 1.1.0 can generate
incorrect byteorder conversions, see 9fe58952c45a,
"evaluate: skip byteorder conversion for selector smaller than 2 bytes"
in nftables.git).  Affected rulesets fail to load with this change and
old userspace due to 'len != size' check.

Issue summary: Encrypting a CMS message to an EC certificate whose group order
is 1 may cause CMS_encrypt() or CMS_encrypt_ex() to loop indefinitely.

Impact summary: An attacker able to supply the recipient certificate to an
application performing CMS encryption can cause that application to loop
indefinitely, consuming CPU and resulting in Denial of Service.

CWE: CWE-835: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop')

Description: CMS_encrypt() and CMS_encrypt_ex() encrypt a message to one or
more recipient certificates and, for an EC recipient, generate an ephemeral
key in the recipient's group. If the certificate declares a group order of 1,
random scalar generation can only produce zero. The key generation routine
then retries without limit while waiting for a nonzero private scalar, so the
call never returns.

The OpenSSL TLS and QUIC implementations do not use this path. An application
is exposed only if it calls CMS_encrypt() or CMS_encrypt_ex() with a recipient
certificate whose EC parameters are attacker-controlled. Certificates with
normal EC group orders do not trigger the loop.

OpenSSL 4.0 and later reject unknown explicit EC groups in default builds.
These versions are affected only when configured with the
enable-ec_explicit_curves option.

The result is a hang that consumes a CPU core until the process is
interrupted, a Denial of Service. The severity is Low because the attacker
must supply the recipient certificate and the application must choose to
encrypt to it; ordinary CMS encryption to trusted recipients is unaffected.

The fix makes EC key generation fail when the group has no valid nonzero
private scalar, instead of retrying indefinitely.

FIPS impact: no
The FIPS modules in 4.1, 4.0, 3.5 and 3.0 are not affected. The FIPS provider
does not support arbitrary explicit EC domain parameters, so an order-1 group
is rejected during key import before the vulnerable key generation path is
reached.

Issue summary: QUIC, when performing automated peer detection, may allow
uninitialized stack data to leak into the received address which is then used
as the destination for outgoing packets.

Impact summary: Applications using QUIC's automated peer detection mechanism
may receive an invalid address, leading to connection loss and disclosure of
uninitialized stack data to an attacker observing the outgoing network traffic.

CWE: CWE-457 (Use of Uninitialized Variable)

Description: The OpenSSL QUIC stack contains a feature in which, when using an
already connected socket, it will auto-detect the peer address during the SSL
handshake.  This feature uses the getpeername() function, passing a buffer of
sufficient length to hold any supported address family, but passes a buffer
length that is only sized such that larger addresses, such as IPv6, cannot be
retrieved. The getpeername() function however, still returns the full address
length, which is accepted as the valid input buffer length, leading to the
address buffer containing uninitialized stack data instead of the actual peer
address. The invalid peer address is then used as destination for the outgoing
packets which leads to a connectivity breakage and a leakage of the
uninitialized stack data to passive network observers.

FIPS impact: no
The FIPS modules in 4.0, 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, and 3.0 are not affected by this CVE as
the affected protocol is not implemented in the FIPS module.

Issue summary: The AES-GCM-SIV implementation treats a zero-length Additional
Authenticated Data (AAD) update as a reset of all the AAD supplied so far,
instead of leaving the AAD unchanged. An application that supplies its AAD in
several fragments, one of which is empty, therefore produces or verifies
messages whose authentication tag does not cover the AAD supplied before
the empty fragment.

Impact summary: Data an application intended to authenticate alongside a
message is silently left unauthenticated. An attacker can forge the AAD of such
a message.

CWE: CWE-325: Missing Cryptographic Step

Description: An application passing AAD in multiple chunks of which some have
zero length will have the previous AAD chunks effectively unauthenticated. Also,
on context re-initialisation, the AAD was not reset, which meant that any AAD
accumulated from the previous context usage were also included in the AAD of the
new message.

The fix makes a zero-length AAD update a no-op and clears any accumulated AAD
whenever the context is re-initialised with a key or a nonce.
A re-initialisation that only changes parameters keeps the AAD.

FIPS impact: no
The FIPS modules are not affected, as AES-GCM-SIV is not a FIPS approved
algorithm and is implemented only in the default provider, outside the
OpenSSL FIPS module boundary.

Impact summary: A malicious QUIC server can cause a heap-use-after-free read
in the OpenSSL QUIC client. The server can also identify one allocator-adjacent
byte through the client's protected Handshake response.

CWE: CWE-416: Use After Free

Description: During CRYPTO stream processing, a pointer into the first frame's
memory on the stream is lent to the TLS handshake processing. The memory
must remain stable until it is processed and released. However the processing
of retransmitted CRYPTO frames could release the memory if the retransmitted
frame fully overlapped the existing frame. This then causes use-after-free read
when the TLS handshake processing continues.

The use-after-free read can lead to a Denial-of-Service of the client
application or a minor leak of information about the heap memory contents
that might be overwritten with other data, subsequently allocated by
the application, to the peer.

FIPS impact: no
The FIPS module is not affected as the QUIC implementation is outside of
the OpenSSL FIPS module boundary.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xen-netback: Fix XenBus connection failure cleanup

xenvif_get_stats and xenvif_get_ethtool_stats capture vif->num_queues
under rcu_read_lock. We need to unpublish vif->num_queues before
synchronize_net to ensure that readers that come afterwards will not
read a non-zero vif->num_queues and attempt to access invalid queues.

This is the same cleanup algorithm as used in backend_disconnect and
added in commit b17075d5c198 ("xen-netback: fix race condition on XenBus
disconnect").

This is XSA-531

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xen-netback: Zero out sring pointers on unmap

If xenvif_map_frontend_data_rings() fails when a ring is already mapped,
it unmaps them via xenvif_unmap_frontend_data_rings() which keeps the
ring pointers unchanged. xenvif_connect_data()'s cleanup path calls
xenvif_disconnect_queue() which in turn calls
xenvif_unmap_frontend_data_rings() again, which will attempt to unmap the
pointers a second time.

Zero out the ring pointers after they are unmapped to avoid this issue.

This is XSA-532

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

inet: reject unhashed sockets during established lookups

TCP established ehash lookups are lockless. The socket caches involved
use SLAB_TYPESAFE_BY_RCU, so memory can be reused before an RCU reader
that retained its old address has finished.

After a tuple match, __inet_lookup_established() and
__inet6_lookup_established() acquire a reference and repeat the tuple
check. They do not check whether the new object is hashed. If the
address is reused for a socket with the same tuple, the lookup can
acquire a reference to the new object and return it while its nulls node
is unhashed.

A PoC that drives reuse with a SYN cookie request socket reproduced the
crash. The new request socket is unhashed and has a NULL rsk_listener.
A lookup that had loaded the address of the old request socket acquired
the reference published by tcp_get_cookie_sock() and returned the new
object. tcp_v4_rcv() then read sk_state through the NULL listener.

The resulting crash was:

  BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000012
  #PF: supervisor read access in kernel mode
  #PF: error_code(0x0000) - not-present page
  ...
  Oops: Oops: 0000 [#1] SMP NOPTI
  CPU: 4 UID: 0 PID: 0 Comm: swapper/4 Not tainted 7.3.0-00591-g0e135910deec #1 PREEMPT(lazy)
  ...
  RIP: 0010:tcp_v4_rcv+0x44e/0x1280
  ...
  R10: 0000000000000001 R11: 00000000024ca8c0 R12: 0000000000000000
  ...
  CR2: 0000000000000012 CR3: 0000000103d50004 CR4: 0000000000770ef0
  ...
  Call Trace:
   <IRQ>
   ? raw_local_deliver+0xae/0x240
   ip_protocol_deliver_rcu+0x2d/0x180
   ip_local_deliver_finish+0x84/0x100
   ip_sublist_rcv_finish+0x5f/0x70
   ip_sublist_rcv+0x12a/0x1d0
   ip_list_rcv+0xfd/0x130
   __netif_receive_skb_list_core+0x223/0x250
   netif_receive_skb_list_internal+0x1d2/0x2c0
   ? try_fill_recv+0x39/0x7b0
   napi_complete_done+0x74/0x170
   virtnet_poll+0x445/0x600
   __napi_poll+0x27/0x1e0
   net_rx_action+0x2fe/0x3b0
   handle_softirqs+0xc2/0x2c0
   __irq_exit_rcu+0x74/0xd0
   common_interrupt+0x7f/0x90
   </IRQ>
  ...
  Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception in interrupt

After taking a reference, check whether the nulls node is unhashed in
both IPv4 and IPv6 established lookups. If it is unhashed or the tuple
no longer matches, drop the reference and restart the lookup.

Lookups racing with the TIME_WAIT hashdance, or with a request being
replaced by its child, now restart and find the new socket instead of
returning the old one.

Request sockets that were never inserted into ehash can have a nonzero
refcount, and a stale lookup can hold a transient reference. Therefore,
when SYN cookie, Fast Open, and request migration paths fail after
setting a nonzero refcount, release the references held by those paths
with reqsk_put() instead of freeing the request directly.

In multiple functions of Android.bp, there is a possible way to bind to a privileged debug overlay service due to test or debugging code. This could lead to local escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

Moby's overlay network driver does not restore the iptables rules for encrypted overlay networks after firewalld deletes them. Unlike other Docker Engine networking components, the overlay driver does not handle firewalld reload or start signals over D-Bus. The missing rules cause outgoing VXLAN datagrams to bypass IPsec encryption and remove the protection against incoming cleartext VXLAN traffic. The condition is not logged by dockerd and persists until the encrypted network's last local endpoint is removed and another is added, or dockerd is restarted. Each further firewalld event repeats the condition.

A use-after-free issue exists in MongoDB’s SBE (Slot-Based Execution) implementation of a window function accumulator used by certain $setWindowFields aggregation pipelines. Under specific conditions, the accumulator can retain a dangling pointer to memory that has since been freed. When this stale pointer is later dereferenced during serialization of the carried-forward value, it can result in a heap out-of-bounds read that may expose adjacent heap contents and crash the mongod server. An authenticated user with readWrite privileges on a database can trigger this issue by crafting a specific aggregation pipeline.

A flaw exists in the server-side SSPI Kerberos authentication handler on Windows Enterprise builds of MongoDB. When processing certain authentication requests, the server fails to properly release an underlying system resource due to an internal tracking error. An unauthenticated user can trigger this by repeatedly sending authentication requests using the Kerberos mechanism, eventually exhausting available resources and causing all subsequent Kerberos authentication attempts to fail. Server restart is required to recover.

In MongoDB Server, an authenticated user with insert privileges on a collection could craft a command with specially constructed encryption-related parameters to redirect internal Queryable Encryption metadata writes to metadata belonging to other encrypted collections within the same database. The server’s authorization layer validated only the user-facing target collection namespace, while subsequent internal writes derived from client-supplied parameters were performed with elevated internal privileges, bypassing the original caller’s permission scope. This could allow unauthorized writes into another collection’s Queryable Encryption metadata, potentially corrupting encrypted index state and compaction operations.

A flaw in MongoDB Server's user management commands may lead to incomplete cleanup of role authorization data when roles are dropped from a database. Due to incorrect internal query predicates, the drop operation removes role definitions but fails to remove stale references in user and role documents. If a role with the same name is subsequently recreated with different privileges, previously associated users may silently inherit the new role's privileges without an explicit grant or corresponding audit event. Exploitation requires authenticated access with database administrative privileges on the target database.

A flaw in MongoDB’s X.509 cluster-membership authentication guard could allow a holder of a cluster-member certificate to gain elevated internal privileges when a specific deployment configuration is in use. An internal check, which prevents a certificate recognized as a cluster member from also being treated as a regular user, does not correctly distinguish between certain error conditions encountered during user lookup. Under certain timing conditions, this can cause the check to be bypassed, granting the connection full internal system privileges. Triggering this issue requires possession of a valid cluster-member TLS certificate, non-default X.509 cluster authentication configuration, and specific conditions during the user cache lookup process.

An issue exists in MongoDB's macOS TLS client implementation where certificate chain-of-trust validation is bypassed for outbound connections to IPv6-addressed peers. When a MongoDB process using the Apple SecureTransport TLS backend connects to an IPv6 target, the trust evaluation result from SecTrustEvaluate is silently discarded, regardless of whether the peer's certificate is trusted. An on-path party could exploit this by presenting a self-signed certificate containing the target's IPv6 address in the Subject Alternative Name to intercept and modify encrypted inter-node or external service traffic. This issue only affects MongoDB processes running on macOS with the Apple SecureTransport TLS provider.

A use-after-free read issue exists in MongoDB’s SBE (Slot-Based Execution) engine when processing aggregation pipelines with $unwind on time-series collections. An internal error in state-preservation logic can cause a value still referenced by downstream stages to have its underlying memory freed prematurely. An authenticated user can craft an aggregation pipeline under specific conditions to trigger this condition, potentially reading recycled server heap memory in query results or crashing the server. This issue is only triggerable when a non-default server parameter related to the SBE engine is enabled.

An issue in MongoDB server’s aggregation framework allows an authenticated user with read privileges to cause a denial of service by sending specially crafted aggregate commands using an internal expression. Despite its internal naming, this expression is registered as accessible to any authenticated client. By supplying crafted input parameters across multiple concurrent connections, each evaluation triggers unbounded memory allocations with no per-expression memory limits enforced. This can exhaust available server memory and cause the mongod process to be terminated by the operating system’s out-of-memory killer.

A use-after-free issue exists in the MongoDB server’s classic query engine plan cache. Under certain query conditions, an unowned reference to data from an earlier command can be retained in cached plan statistics. After the originating memory is freed, a subsequent diagnostic command serializing those statistics can read freed heap memory, potentially returning sensitive server process memory contents to the authenticated client. Under certain heap reuse conditions, this may also cause the server to crash.

An issue in MongoDB Server's query processing component allows an authenticated user with read privileges to cause a denial of service. Uncontrolled recursion in an internal query compilation component can lead to stack exhaustion and server process termination when processing certain queries against time-series collections.

An issue in MongoDB Server's client-side field-level encryption (CSFLE) schema processing component allows encryption metadata to be silently dropped during schema parsing under certain conditions. A party who can deliver a specially crafted schema to a user's CSFLE client may cause sensitive data intended for encryption to be stored in plaintext, bypassing confidentiality protections. Exploitation requires the ability to deliver the malicious schema to the user's client, such as through a man-in-the-middle position or an untrusted server.

An improper privilege management issue in the sharding subsystem of MongoDB Server may allow a user holding certain shard-level administrative privileges to cause persisted internal coordination state to be reprocessed with elevated internal authority. Because that state is trusted rather than re-validated, operations may be carried out beyond the user's authorized scope, including changes to cluster-wide security configuration. Successful triggering this issue requires an authenticated session directly against a cluster member and can result in unauthorized access to and modification of data across the cluster.

An incorrect authorization check in the MongoDB Server authorization subsystem may allow an unauthenticated party with local host access to obtain administrative privileges on a database server that has authorization enabled. This may result in unintended access to stored data and credentials, unintended modification of data, and loss of availability of the server.

Winter CMS is a content management system built on the Laravel PHP framework. Prior to 1.2.14, BrandSetting::renderCss() and EditorSetting::renderCss() store raw LESS compiler output with Cache::forever() but apply strip_tags() only to the value returned on a cache miss. The first render after saving custom CSS appears sanitized while priming an unsafe cache entry, and later cache hits return unsanitized output into the backend style element, allowing a user with backend.manage_branding or backend.manage_editor to cause stored cross-site scripting when another backend page renders the styles. The styles also appear on unauthenticated backend sign-in, password restore, and password reset layouts. This issue is fixed in version 1.2.14.

Winter CMS is a content management system built on the Laravel PHP framework. From 1.0.420 until 1.2.14, the backend Table widget partial modules/backend/widgets/table/partials/_table.php emits the search query parameter without HTML encoding inside a script template. A script-closing sequence in a crafted top-level GET URL terminates the raw-text template and causes the remaining input to be parsed as backend markup, even when the widget uses searching: false.
