In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: smbdirect: release failed pending sockets of a listener

A child of a listener only left the listen.pending or listen.ready
list via smbdirect_socket_accept() or when the listener was
destroyed. So every connection that failed before it was accepted
(negotiate timeout, peer disconnect, invalid negotiate request, ...)
stayed on the list and counted against the backlog until the listener
was destroyed. After about backlog (10 for ksmbd) such connections
smbdirect_listen_connect_request() rejected every new connection with
-EBUSY, so an unauthenticated peer was able to permanently stop
ksmbd from accepting SMB-Direct connections.

Now a failed child moves itself to a new listen.orphaned list at the
end of smbdirect_socket_cleanup_work(), after the disconnect was
started, and queues listen.purge_orphaned_work, which releases it
with smbdirect_socket_release(), without holding the listener's
rdma_lock_handler() lock, in the same way smbdirect_socket_destroy()
does for the remaining children. Orphaned sockets still count against
the backlog until they are released.

sc->accept.listener is now only changed under listener->listen.lock
and whoever clears it is responsible for releasing the socket:
smbdirect_socket_accept(), purge_orphaned_work or the destroy of the
listener.

In order to make that work:

- a struct smbdirect_socket that is a listener is now freed via
  kfree_rcu(), so that a child can dereference sc->accept.listener
  under rcu_read_lock(), even if the listener is released concurrently.

- smbdirect_listen_connect_request() adds nsc to the listen.pending
  list and sets nsc->accept.listener before it calls
  smbdirect_accept_connect_request(), and always returns 0 so the
  rdma_cm core keeps the connection id and nsc owns it. On a non-zero
  return it schedules nsc's teardown with
  smbdirect_socket_schedule_cleanup(), which orphans it off the
  listener so that purge_orphaned_work releases it; nsc destroys its
  own connection id with rdma_destroy_id() in that teardown. The
  teardown has to be deferred because the rdma_cm core holds nsc's
  id_priv->handler_mutex across the handler, so nsc->rdma.cm_id must
  not be destroyed synchronously from here. That same handler_mutex
  (and the listener's) also guarantees nsc can't go away under us,
  so setting the listener before the call is safe and lets a failure
  orphan nsc.

- smbdirect_accept_negotiate_recv_work() no longer moves a socket to
  the ready list if it already failed or no longer belongs to the
  listener. Every accepting socket has a listener, so if
  sc->accept.listener is already cleared, it no longer sends a
  negotiate response, as the socket is about to be released.

- smbdirect_socket_destroy() of the listener disables
  purge_orphaned_work and also releases the orphaned sockets.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: smbdirect: don't wait for RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED in smbdirect_socket_destroy_sync()

smbdirect_socket_destroy_sync() waited for RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED
after smbdirect_socket_cleanup_work() called rdma_disconnect(). That
can take very long, e.g. if the peer just disappeared, until the
rdma cm gives up, or forever if the event already happened, but the
status was overwritten afterwards.

This is not needed: smbdirect_socket_destroy() drains the qp under
rdma_lock_handler(), destroys it and calls rdma_destroy_id(), which
only waits for a currently running event handler and makes sure no
further events are delivered. The rest of the disconnect protocol
(DREQ/DREP and timewait for IB, abrupt close for iWarp) is handled
by the rdma core asynchronously. drivers/nvme/host/rdma.c also just
calls rdma_disconnect() and ib_drain_qp() before rdma_destroy_id().

So smbdirect_socket_destroy() now also accepts
SMBDIRECT_SOCKET_DISCONNECTING and changes the status to
SMBDIRECT_SOCKET_DISCONNECTED itself under rdma_lock_handler().

We could still get RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED in the small
windows between rdma_unlock_handler() and rdma_destroy_id(),
but in that case smbdirect_connection_rdma_event_handler()
is basically a no-op.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: wait for negotiation before receiving another PDU

The receive thread queues a request and can read the next PDU before
the negotiation worker finishes. While need_neg is set, the next PDU
can cause ksmbd_init_smb_server() to replace conn->ops. A pipelined
SMB2 request can therefore make the worker handle an earlier, shorter
SMB1 request with SMB2 operations and read beyond its buffer.

An SMB1 multi-protocol negotiate may be followed by an SMB2 NEGOTIATE
that changes conn->ops again. Wait for work queued while the connection
is new or needs negotiation to complete before reading another PDU.
This keeps the operations stable for both stages of negotiation without
changing when need_neg is cleared.

Mattermost Plugins versions <=12.-1 11.11.7 11.2.10 11.1.11.0 fail to enforce the GitLab project permission check for confidential issues when the project is publicly visible which allows an authenticated user with no GitLab membership in the project to obtain the contents of confidential issues, including title, description, author, and URL via subscribing a channel to the parent public GitLab group with the confidential_issues feature and waiting for a confidential issue webhook event. Mattermost Advisory ID: MMSA-2026-00738

modified eCommerce Shopsoftware through 3.3.0 contains a local file inclusion vulnerability that allows administrators to include arbitrary server files by storing ../ sequences in the content manager file name. Unauthenticated requests to shop_content.php then pass the stored path to include(), executing embedded PHP in uploaded content files or images as the web server user.

modified eCommerce Shopsoftware through 3.3.0 contains a reflected cross-site scripting vulnerability in admin/support.php that allows unauthenticated attackers to inject script via the module parameter. Attackers can trick a logged-in administrator into opening a crafted link to run script in the admin panel, reading CSRF tokens and changing shop settings.
In JetBrains YouTrack before 2026.2.19840 improper authorization allowed project administrators to obtain GitLab tokens of other projects

Joomla Extension - vi-solutions - Arbitrary file write leading to remote code execution in CSS editor in Visforms extension 1.0.0-5.6.3, 6.0.0-6.2.0 - The CSS editor did not restrict file names, extensions and paths of created and saved files, allowing privileged backend users to write arbitrary PHP files.

Joomla Extension - vi-solutions - Code injection via calculation formulas in Visforms extension 1.0.0-5.6.4, 6.0.0-6.2.1 - Calculation field formulas were executed using PHP eval() without validating their content, allowing backend users with field edit permissions to execute arbitrary PHP code.

A command injection vulnerability was found in OpenStack Cinder's SSH-based storage-driver support. Incomplete validation of shell metacharacters allows an authenticated user who owns a volume on an affected backend to supply crafted connection information and inject additional commands into the storage array's management interface. Commands execute with the privileges of Cinder's configured backend account. This can disclose storage configuration information and, where that account has administrative permissions, could allow changes that affect the integrity or availability of other tenants' storage.

Jupyter MCP Server is a Model Context Protocol server for Jupyter. Prior to 1.0.3, standalone streamable-http mode validates Host and Origin values for /mcp but does not apply the same browser-origin controls to the state-changing /api/connect and /api/stop management routes. A malicious website can use DNS rebinding so that its hostname resolves to a loopback, LAN, VPN, or published-container MCP listener, then send a browser-shaped request that /api/connect accepts to replace runtime_url and document_url values and start a kernel client against attacker-controlled infrastructure. The attacker can thereby cause Jupyter API and WebSocket traffic to reach that infrastructure and can use /api/stop to stop the current notebook kernel. The default broad bind can increase exposure, but the vulnerability is the missing management-route origin boundary, not a lack of Host validation on /mcp. This issue is fixed in version 1.0.3.

InfoScan uses hard-coded cryptographic keys and initialization-vector values in its database-encryption implementation. The application uses these values to encrypt the MongoDB password before storing it in the Windows registry. Because the cryptographic material is embedded in the distributed application, an individual with access to the encrypted registry value and the application code may be able to recover the database password.

Paymenter is a free and open-source webshop solution for management of hosting services. Prior to 1.5.7, the HasConfirmation trait in app/Livewire/Traits/HasConfirmation.php, included by app/Livewire/Component.php across 36 client-facing Livewire components, exposed executeConfirmedAction as a public action that invoked any component method accepted by method_exists. The action could call inherited InteractsWithProperties::fill(), whose data_set() writes arbitrary public properties, including state marked with #[Locked] and dotted paths into hydrated Eloquent models. Depending on the methods and properties exposed by an individual component, an unauthenticated caller could use this path to bypass intended authorization and modify server-side state intended to be immutable or protected from client-side manipulation. This issue is fixed in version 1.5.7.

TeamPass is a self-hosted collaborative password manager. Prior to 3.2.1.2, the update_folder action in app/sources/folders.queries.php allowed an authenticated, non-read-only user to re-parent a folder without checking whether the target folder or submitted parentId belonged to the caller's user-accessible_folders set. Selecting a personal folder as the new parent passed the personal-folder guard and set personal_folder on the target, transferring the credential subtree into the attacker's accessible space after the next login and hiding it from the organization, including administrators. The change exposed credential labels, logins, URLs, email addresses, and descriptions, while sharekey-protected passwords remained protected; hiding the subtree also denied other users access. This issue is fixed in version 3.2.1.2.

pREST (PostgreSQL REST) is an API that delivers an application on top of a Postgres database. Prior to 2.4.0, the vulnerable parameter is _groupby, handled by GroupByClause in adapters/postgres/postgres.go. adapters/postgres/postgres.go uses the weaker isSafeSQLExpression check for this function-expression branch instead of the stricter single-field validator used for _select. That check validates only the outer function name against a 13-function allowlist and permits nested subqueries, trailing UNION syntax, and inner pg_ functions. controllers/crud.go concatenates the GROUP BY expression while parameterizing only WHERE values, allowing attacker-controlled SQL structure into the clause. Default configuration permits unauthenticated access; a restricted installation may require a low-privilege table reader. UNION-based extraction requires compatible column counts and types and was not verified end to end, but a delay-producing function can cause denial of service without that alignment. This issue is fixed in 2.4.0.

@fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. In versions before 11.6.10, it rejects destinations containing parent-directory path segments by an exact string match, so a segment that carries a semicolon path parameter, such as a dot-dot segment followed by a semicolon and an optional parameter, is not equal to the plain dot-dot form and passes the check, and the WHATWG URL parser keeps it as an ordinary segment so the rewrite-prefix containment check also passes. Servlet containers such as Apache Tomcat and Jetty strip semicolon path parameters from each segment before resolving dot-segments, so a request routed through the configured prefix is rewritten and reaches the upstream where it resolves above the intended subtree, escaping the path the proxy is meant to expose and, on some containers, crossing application contexts. Both the HTTP and WebSocket proxy paths are affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.10, and users should upgrade to 11.6.10 or later.

@fastify/reply-from is a Fastify plugin that forwards requests to an upstream HTTP server. In versions before 12.8.4, its buildURL function rejects parent-directory path segments by an exact string match, so a segment that carries a semicolon path parameter, such as a dot-dot segment followed by a semicolon and an optional parameter, is not equal to the plain dot-dot form and passes the traversal check, and the WHATWG URL parser keeps it as an ordinary segment so the base-prefix containment check also passes. Backends that strip semicolon path parameters before resolving dot-segments, such as Apache Tomcat, Jetty, WildFly, and Spring Boot, turn the segment back into a parent-directory reference and resolve it, so an unauthenticated client can escape the intended upstream prefix and reach internal paths such as admin or internal API endpoints, including with state-changing methods. Deployments that proxy to Node.js, nginx, or Express upstreams are not affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/reply-from 12.8.4, and users should upgrade to 12.8.4 or later.

RepoManager is a self-hosted deb/rpm package repository. Prior to 5.13.3, the authenticated get-unit-log action accepts a caller-controlled logfile value. Validate::string() escapes HTML but leaves path traversal components unchanged. The action joins the caller-controlled logfile to SERVICE_LOGS_DIR without enforcing containment, so traversal can resolve the file read outside that directory. www/controllers/ajax/status/service.php reads and returns the resolved file, and any authenticated user can invoke the action to retrieve files readable by the www-data service account, including application configuration, source code, and the GPG signing-key passphrase. Fixed in 5.13.3.

RepoManager is a self-hosted deb/rpm package repository. Prior to 5.13.3, an authenticated user can supply a user-controlled, array-valued GPG key identifier to the key deletion action. Validate::string() filters HTML characters but not shell metacharacters. The user-controlled identifier reaches the delete action without shell-safe encoding. controllers/Gpg.php contains the vulnerable deletion path. Process::execute() passes the command string through proc_open() and /bin/sh -c, allowing the attacker to execute arbitrary OS commands as the web/PHP process. This can expose secrets or poison packages. Authentication is required, but the advisory makes an administrator-only restriction conditional on the intended access policy and does not establish an administrator role as a prerequisite. Fixed in 5.13.3.

@fastify/reply-from is a Fastify plugin that forwards requests to an upstream HTTP server. In versions 12.8.1 through 12.8.3, its buildURL function checked the attacker-supplied source string for parent-directory segments, but when the source begins with the same special scheme as the base, such as http or https, the WHATWG URL parser drops the scheme and resolves the remainder as a relative path. A payload that glues the scheme to a percent-encoded parent-directory sequence therefore passes the check, because the inspected segment reads as the scheme plus the dots rather than a bare parent-directory token, while the proxy forwards the encoded traversal unchanged. An upstream that percent-decodes the request path before resolving dot-segments then serves a path outside the configured prefix, so an unauthenticated client scoped to an upstream prefix, or relying on Fastify route guards in front of the proxy, can escape that prefix and reach sibling or parent upstream endpoints. The per-segment check added in 12.8.1 is what the scheme prefix bypasses, and releases up to 12.8.0 already rejected the decoded form. The issue is fixed in @fastify/reply-from 12.8.4, and users should upgrade to 12.8.4 or later.

Poweradmin is a web-based DNS administration tool for PowerDNS server. From 4.0.0 until 4.2.6, 4.3.5, and 4.4.1, lib/Domain/Service/MfaService.php verifies email second-factor codes through MfaService::verifyCode() without limiting failed attempts, and lib/Application/Controller/MfaVerifyController.php logs failures without throttling them. An attacker who knows the user's password can repeatedly guess the six-digit code during its ten-minute validity period when email MFA is enabled, potentially bypassing the second factor; the advisory notes MFA is disabled by default and that the practical request rate was not measured. This issue is fixed in versions 4.2.6, 4.3.5, and 4.4.1.

The MongoDB Rust Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

The MongoDB Ruby driver can include unmasked connection string content in the error it raises when a connection string cannot be parsed. If that connection string carries a secret, the secret may be disclosed in cleartext through the application's error output or logs. No privileges on the driver and no network access are needed to produce the error; a party able to read the application's error output may obtain the secret.

The MongoDB Ruby Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

The MongoDB Python Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

A credential-handling weakness in the MongoDB Python Driver allows a configuration option value that protects private key material to be written in clear text into the embedding application's own output and log records when a driver object is converted to text. A party able to read that output may obtain the credential. Obtaining it requires read access to the application's local output or log files.

The MongoDB PHP extension includes the full connection string it was given in the error it raises when that string cannot be parsed. A party able to influence any part of the connection string, including a part that holds no secret, can cause the resulting message to carry credentials into the application's standard error output and log files. This may result in unintended disclosure of authentication material to anyone able to read that output.

The MongoDB Node.js Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

A weakness in the MongoDB Node.js driver can place sensitive information taken from an application-supplied connection string into the text of an error produced while that connection string is being parsed. The error is generated inside the application process before any database connection is made, so no database account and no network access are needed for it to occur. A party able to read the application's error output or log files may thereby obtain database credentials that the application's configuration source would otherwise keep to a narrower audience.

The MongoDB Go driver's connection string parser includes the raw, undecoded value of a query option in the error it returns when that value contains invalid percent encodings. When the option holds a secret, such as a TLS key file password or an AWS session token, the secret appears in plain text in the error. A party with low-privileged read access to wherever the application records or displays that error may learn the secret.

The MongoDB Go Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

A MongoDB C# Driver component that interprets connection configuration supplied by the hosting application can include the caller-supplied configuration value in the text of the error it raises when that value cannot be interpreted. The redaction applied to that text does not cover all forms in which secret material may appear, so authentication material embedded in the configuration value can be preserved in the resulting error text and in anything that records it. Exploitation requires only the low privilege needed to observe the application's own error output or logs on the system where the driver runs; no database credentials or server connectivity are required. The result is disclosure of sensitive information to parties whose access to error output is broader than their intended access to the configuration secret.

The MongoDB C# Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

An improper neutralization of delimiters in the MongoDB C# driver's DNS SRV connection-string resolution lets an unauthenticated party who can answer the client's DNS SRV query place a host outside the trusted domain into the client's server list. When an application resolves the connection string through the affected API and connects with the result, application data, authentication credentials and query results may pass through that host. This may result in unintended disclosure of data and credentials and in forged query results.

The MongoDB C Driver places a submitted connection-string option value into a diagnostic message without redaction when that option fails validation. The message is returned to the calling application and is also written to the process's standard error by the driver's default logging behavior. A party that can influence the connection string given to an application using the driver may cause that field's contents to be recorded, which may result in unintended disclosure of information the application placed in that field.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the mc_investigation_read capability could overwrite Mission Control preference records for other users and remove saved filters and analyst queue settings from those records.
The vulnerability is possible because the Mission Control user preferences Representational State Transfer (REST) API does not bind an update to the preference record that passes the authorization check.
The attack requires the user to obtain a preference record identifier that the product does not normally expose to that user. The user should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.
For more information see Overview of Mission Control in Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/user-guide/8.7/mission-control/overview-of-mission-control-in-splunk-enterprise-security) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with the System Settings view and edit permissions could test a Lightweight Directory Access Protocol authentication provider and cause Splunk SOAR to send a stored directory service account bind password to a host that the user controls.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR reuses a stored directory service provider credential when an authentication test uses a different directory service connection destination.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with container edit permission could supply timestamps when creating containers and artifacts through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API. This could alter the timeline shown to analysts and cause configured data retention strategies to delete affected records earlier than intended.
The vulnerability is possible because the REST API accepts client-supplied values for timestamps that Splunk SOAR uses to order records and apply data retention.
The early deletion impact requires an applicable data retention strategy; the timeline impact does not.
For more information see Manage your PostgreSQL database with data retention strategies (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/6.4.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-system-health-and-performance/manage-your-postgresql-database-with-data-retention-strategies) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user who can edit and run playbooks could cause automation batches for other events to stop running.
The vulnerability occurs because Splunk SOAR does not bind playbook API requests to the server-provided execution context.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with the Playbooks view, edit, execute, and delete permissions could cause existing cross-repository playbook references to run attacker-controlled playbook code.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR can bind existing cross-repository playbook references to a different source control repository when a deleted repository name is reused.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user with permission to edit and run playbooks could view child playbook status and loop-state metadata for playbook runs outside the authorized scope for that user.
The vulnerability is possible because the playbook status API does not bind the requested run to the current execution context before it returns metadata.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user with permission to edit and run playbooks could read or overwrite persisted data for playbook runs outside the authorized label, or ownership scope for that user. The affected data can include playbook inputs, prompt and block results, outputs, and secrets that playbooks save in run data. Overwriting the data could corrupt results that paused, scheduled, or parent playbook runs later use.
The vulnerability is possible because the playbook automation APIs do not bind data operations to the active playbook run.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user who can edit and run playbooks on a container label could associate a custom-function callback with another playbook run. The callback could modify the state of a container outside the authorized scope for that user.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not bind playbook API requests to the trusted playbook run and container context.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user with permission to create and run playbooks could start child playbooks on containers outside the authorized label, or repository scope for that user. This could expose container data and affect automation outside that scope.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not bind the identity used to authorize the child playbook run to the parent playbook execution context.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an operator of a configured identity provider could authenticate as an existing user associated with another configured identity provider. If that account has the "Administrator" Splunk SOAR role, the operator could control the Splunk SOAR deployment.
Splunk SOAR does not bind external user accounts to the identity provider that provisions them and authenticates accounts by username without verifying provider ownership.
The vulnerability requires more than one configured external identity provider with distinct trust domains and a target username that an operator of a configured identity provider can authenticate through a different provider.
For more information see Configure single sign-on authentication (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.7.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/configure-single-sign-on-authentication-for-splunk-soar-on-premises) and Manage roles and permissions (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.8.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/manage-roles-and-permissions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17 on Ubuntu and AlmaLinux, an unauthenticated user who obtains a valid Splunk Web session cookie before the affected user logs out could continue using the cookie after logout to access data and perform actions available to that user.
The vulnerability is possible because the logout flow does not invalidate the associated session token on affected deployments.
The attacker must obtain the valid session cookie before the affected user logs out of Splunk Web. The issue was reproduced in Splunk Enterprise installations on Ubuntu and AlmaLinux.

Connaisseur is an admission controller that integrates container image signature verification into a Kubernetes cluster. Prior to 3.11.1, the Cosign validator counts valid signature layers rather than distinct trust roots for trustRoot: "*" policies using an explicit threshold or an implicit require-all policy. An attacker who controls one configured trust root's signing key and can attach multiple signatures to an image can satisfy a threshold intended to require multiple independent roots, causing admission without the intended signer quorum. Policies using a single trust root or the required option are not affected. This issue is fixed in 3.11.1.

A component of the MongoDB Java Driver that processes connection configuration places credential values taken from that configuration into generated text and error output without replacing them with a placeholder, unlike other parts of the driver. A party able to read output produced by an application that embeds the driver may obtain database or proxy credentials in clear text.

The MongoDB Java driver applies its DNS seedlist domain restriction to a record value that is later re-interpreted differently when the connection target is parsed, so the name that is checked and the name that is used can differ. An unauthenticated party who can set or forge the DNS service record for the seed domain in a connection string can cause the driver to direct its session to an unrelated host and to complete certificate verification against that host instead. This may result in unintended disclosure of application data and of configured database credentials, and in unintended content being returned to the application as query results.

The MongoDB Java Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

Insufficient verification of data authenticity in the decryption component of Amazon S3 Encryption Client for PHP in AWS SDK for PHP before 3.383.1 might allow an authenticated remote user to forge ciphertext that decrypts to arbitrary plaintext via manipulation of the GCM authentication tag length metadata.



To remediate this issue, users should upgrade to AWS SDK for PHP version 3.383.1 or later.

A vulnerability was determined in smartalock wireguard-lwip up to cfba91666590e86bd67842c71cedf9a423be823a. Impacted is the function mul of the file src/crypto/refc/x25519.c of the component X25519 Ladder. Executing a manipulation can lead to out-of-bounds write. The attack can be executed remotely. This product implements a rolling release for ongoing delivery, which means version information for affected or updated releases is unavailable. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

baserCMS is a website development framework. From 5.2.3 until 5.3.0, BcThemeFileService::getFullpath() in plugins/bc-theme-file/src/Service/BcThemeFileService.php skips its path containment check when realpath() fails for a nonexistent theme subdirectory selected by the type parameter. An authenticated administrator can supply a traversal path through the theme-file API to access locations outside the theme directory. The bypass of the CVE-2026-30940 fix can permit file writes, overwrites or deletion within the PHP process permissions and, where executable PHP can be written, remote code execution. This issue is fixed in 5.3.0.

baserCMS is a website development framework. Prior to 5.3.0, getAuthenticationService permits an Api/Admin session authentication fallback based on the Referer header, although operator accounts have an Admin auth prefix and cannot obtain an Api/Admin JWT. An authenticated operator can therefore access /baser/api/admin/ endpoints whose permission.php entries have auth => true, including /baser/api/admin/baser-core/site_configs/view.json, even when the corresponding administrative functionality is restricted. This can disclose administrator-restricted configuration information. This issue is fixed in 5.3.0.

IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 is vulnerable to improper TLS certificate validation in the GDP Terraform provider, allowing a network attacker with a man-in-the-middle position to intercept sensitive credentials transmitted to the Guardium appliance.

Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in Apache Tomcat could occur during a request dispatch if the request depended on a security-role-ref provided by the dispatch target.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

assoc_array: keep gc's cleanup out of the live tree on allocation failure

assoc_array_gc() builds a copy of the tree.  Where the copy reaches a
shortcut, it allocates the copy of the shortcut with kmalloc_flex(),
fills it with memcpy(), links it into the new tree, and only then
allocates the copy of the node after it.  The memcpy() leaves the new
shortcut's next_node pointing at the old tree's node, so if that second
allocation fails, the cleanup, assoc_array_destroy_subtree() on the new
tree, follows the new shortcut into the old tree, and the BUG_ON() on
the old node's back pointer fires.

Allocate the node first, and the shortcut once the node exists, freeing
the node again if the shortcut cannot be allocated.  A copied shortcut
is then only linked into the new tree when the copy of its node is there
to follow it.  Nothing else changes: with no allocation failing, the
trees gc builds are the same as before.

Found by a userspace test that makes each allocation of each operation
fail in turn.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

assoc_array: don't chain a new shortcut onto an existing one

When a full node's leaves and the new key all share the node's segment,
assoc_array_insert_into_terminal_node() replaces the node with a
shortcut to a pair of new nodes.  If the node is itself the target of a
shortcut, the new shortcut is installed as that shortcut's next node,
and a shortcut leading to a shortcut is something nothing expects:
assoc_array_walk() indexes the second one as a node, and
assoc_array_apply_edit() hits the BUG_ON() in the loop that adjusts
nr_leaves_on_branch, on that same insertion.

Deletion gets a node there.  When the subtree below a shortcut shrinks
enough, assoc_array_delete() collapses it into one node below the
shortcut, and the leaves it collects can all share that node's segment.
The next key that shares it too takes this path.  Eighteen insertions
and a deletion are enough: sixteen keys that agree on bits 0-11, one
that leaves them at bit 8 and is deleted again, and one more that agrees
with the sixteen.

Have the new shortcut replace the one in front of the node as well.
assoc_array_insert_shortcut() gives it that shortcut's back pointer and
parent slot, so the caller installs it where that one was, and excises
the old shortcut along with the node, which takes a second entry in
excised_meta[].  The new shortcut's index key comes from the new key up
to the new skip level, so it covers what the old one did.

Found by a userspace test doing random insertions and deletions on keys
that share long prefixes; a targeted case builds a shortcut, deletes
down to the collapse and inserts one more key.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iommufd/iova_bitmap: Ensure that iova_bitmap_set() handles the full IOVA

Generally userspace is going to step the dirty bitmap through the IOVA
space. However if the bitmap ends in the middle of a large PTE this is
problematic. The first step will clear the dirty bit and report dirty to
the end of its bitmap while the second step will see the clear'd dirty and
report clean for the start of the bitmap. If it happens this ends up
losing dirties.

Further this function is missing bounds checking so if this does happen
ther is a good chance it will write memory beyond what the userspace was
expecting.

Return an error code if this illegal condition happens.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: release a removed xattr node in roll-forward recovery

When xattrs shrink enough to fit in the inline xattr area,
write_all_xattrs() truncates the xattr node and clears i_xattr_nid. If
the file is then fsynced without a checkpoint, only the inode block is
written, with i_xattr_nid of 0.

Roll-forward recovery starts from the checkpointed inode, whose
i_xattr_nid still points to the old xattr node.
f2fs_recover_inline_xattr() copies only the inline xattr area, and
f2fs_update_inode() writes the old i_xattr_nid back. So the inode keeps
the stale xattr node:

 - The node block is never released, and fsck reports "nonzero bytes in
   xattr space after end of list".
 - If the inline xattr list ends exactly at the end of the inline area,
   its terminator is read from the stale node, and the removed xattrs
   come back after recovery.

When the fsynced inode has no xattr node but the checkpointed one has,
release the old xattr node as truncate_node() does: check its block
address, invalidate the block and drop its node cache, which may still
be dirty.

  do_write_block+0x155/0xc10
  f2fs_outplace_write_data+0x192/0x340
  f2fs_do_write_data_page+0xc57/0x1880
  f2fs_write_single_data_page+0xda9/0x15a0
  f2fs_write_cache_pages+0x973/0x1f20

  writeback_sb_inodes+0x67d/0x17a0
  wb_writeback+0x207/0x820
  wb_workfn+0x128/0xc30
  process_one_work+0x925/0x1600
  worker_thread+0x60a/0xff0
  kthread+0x35f/0x460
  ret_from_fork+0x474/0x7e0
  ret_from_fork_asm+0x1a/0x30
  </TASK>

The BUG is f2fs_bug_on(sbi, curseg->next_blkoff >= BLKS_PER_SEG(sbi))
in f2fs_allocate_data_block(), next_blkoff was 512.

The root cause is a race in between atomic write commit and shutdown
as below:

Thread A (commit atomic write)  Thread B (shutdown)        Thread C (writeback)
- f2fs_ioc_commit_atomic_write
 - f2fs_commit_atomic_write
  - __f2fs_commit_atomic_write
   - __replace_atomic_write_block
    - f2fs_replace_block
     - __f2fs_replace_block
                                - f2fs_ioc_shutdown
                                 - f2fs_do_shutdown
                                 : F2FS_GOING_DOWN_METASYNC
                                  - f2fs_sync_fs
                                                           - f2fs_write_single_data_page
                                                           : pass f2fs_cp_error() check
                                  - f2fs_stop_checkpoint
                                  : set CP_ERROR_FLAG
      - change_curseg
       - reset_curseg
       : curseg->segno = new_segno
       : curseg->alloc_type = SSR
       : curseg->next_blkoff = __next_free_blkoff()
         which is BLKS_PER_SEG if there is no free
         slot in new_segno
       - f2fs_get_sum_cache
       : return -EIO due to f2fs_cp_error()
      : return error w/o restoring curseg
     : goto out_unlock, skip restoring
       old segno, blkoff and alloc_type
                                                            - f2fs_do_write_data_page
                                                             - f2fs_outplace_write_data
                                                              - do_write_block
                                                               - f2fs_allocate_data_block
                                                               : curseg->segno is valid
                                                               : f2fs_bug_on(next_blkoff >=
                                                                 BLKS_PER_SEG)

Since commit 86f33603f8c5 ("f2fs: handle errors of
f2fs_get_meta_page_nofail"), change_curseg() can fail after the curseg
has already been switched to the new segment, then the curseg is left
in an inconsistent state: it points to a segment which may have no
free slot, its summary block is zeroed, and the caller can not restore
it. Subsequent block allocation on the curseg will trigger the BUG.
Moreover, the writeback thread dies with curseg_lock, curseg_mutex and
sentry_lock held, so the commit, shutdown and other I/O threads hang
in D state.

Since change_curseg() only fails once CP_ERROR_FLAG is set, no
checkpoint will be committed afterward, let's invalidate the curseg via
reset_curseg_fields() on failure, as new_curseg() does for -ENOSPC,
then f2fs_allocate_data_block() will fail with -ENOSPC on the curseg
instead of triggering BUG, and do_write_block() can handle the error
since CP_ERROR_FLA

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvme-tcp: Validate the queue state under the queue lock in the address attribute

Reading the "address" sysfs attribute calls kernel_getsockname() on the
admin queue socket, which can race with the queue teardown during
connection error recovery: a reader can observe NVME_TCP_Q_LIVE set,
then block on the queue lock while nvme_tcp_free_queue() releases the
socket and clears queue->sock without holding the lock.  Once the
reader acquires the lock it dereferences the NULL socket pointer.

Commit 76d54bf20cdc ("nvme-tcp: don't access released socket during
error recovery") had the queue liveness check inside the lock.
Commit 782373ba2766 ("nvme: tcp: avoid race between queue_lock lock
and destroy") moved it back out because the lock itself is destroyed
in nvme_tcp_free_queue(), so a reader arriving late trips
mutex_destroy().

Check the queue liveness inside the queue lock, and clear queue->sock
under the same lock.  The teardown clears NVME_TCP_Q_LIVE under the
lock well before the socket is released, so a reader either sees the
bit cleared or a socket that cannot be released while it holds the
lock.  To also close the lock lifetime race, the queue locks are now
owned by the controller: they are initialized with the queue array and
only destroyed when the controller is freed, which cannot happen while
a sysfs attribute read is still in progress.  The queue count is
computed by the NVME_TCP_OPT_NR_QUEUES() macro from the original
connect options for both initialization and destruction, as reconnects
may shrink ctrl->queue_count.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: arm64: vgic: Stop the target vcpu when disabling LPIs

Disabling LPIs is pretty nasty, as it directly messes with the AP list
of the affected CPU, which could be running... This has the potential to
lead to really bad behaviours, and we should not be doing that.

Take example on the way the Active state is handled and simply pause the

safely manipulated.

Nobody has any expectation of performance for this anyway.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: bound the SIT/NAT bitmaps by the checkpoint pack

sit_ver_bitmap_bytesize and nat_ver_bitmap_bytesize are used as memcpy
lengths into and out of sbi->ckpt, which is sized from cp_payload alone,
and nothing compares either length against that allocation.

sanity_check_ckpt() has checked these two fields since c77ec61ca0a4, which
added them after a crafted image overran build_sit_info(). That check ties
each length to a segment count; it never compares either against the
allocation, which is the half this adds.

Mounting over-reads in build_sit_info() and build_node_manager(), and the
first checkpoint writes the same lengths back through the same pointers,
so the over-read's contents reach the on-disk checkpoint. An unmount is
enough; the filesystem does not have to be used.

Bound both ends the way __bitmap_ptr() lays them out. The three branches
differ, so a single sum of the two lengths would still admit a small
overflow when cp_payload is non-zero.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: return -EIO for a lost inode block after cp_error

After cp_error, dirty node caches are dropped without being written.
If such an inode was never written, its NAT entry is still NEW_ADDR,
and reading its inode block returns -ENOENT.

f2fs_get_dnode_of_data() passes that -ENOENT up, and callers take it
as a hole. Since the inode block is missing, the next offset can only
advance one block, so fiemap walks block by block up to maxbytes,
about 2^30 blocks, while holding the inode lock. It took hours in a
power-off recovery test after shutdown and blocked unlink and umount
on the file.

Return -EIO instead of -ENOENT when the inode block itself is missing
after cp_error or shutdown. A missing direct or indirect node is still
reported as -ENOENT.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: zone: fix to avoid bio split on sequential zone

In the block layer, bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio if it exceeds
any underlying queue limits:
1. queue_max_sectors: Splits bios larger than the transfer limit. This
   limit is set by the device driver/DMA controller (max_hw_sectors) and
   device-mapper targets. When flushing dirty pages (governed by VFS
   writeback_chunk_size() and f2fs nr_pages_to_skip()), f2fs merges
   contiguous pages into bios up to 512KB (1024 sectors) or more without
   checking queue_max_sectors, which will be split if the device or DM
   target enforces a smaller limit.
2. queue_max_segments: Splits bios exceeding scatter-gather segment
   limits. f2fs allocates bios with up to 256 pages, exceeding the
   128-segment limit of DM targets (dm-default-key/dm-crypt) if pages
   are discontiguous.
3. chunk_sectors: Splits bios crossing chunk/zone boundaries. In f2fs,
   section_size strictly matches zone_size, and block allocation never
   spans across section boundaries, so bios never cross chunk_sectors.

Crucially, when bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio, bio_submit_split()
submits the tail half via submit_bio_noacct() before returning the head
half to the caller. On a sequential zoned device, this causes the tail
bio to arrive at the zone write plug before the head:

  dm-3: zone 7: prepare_bio wp mismatch: bio sector 30720 offset 2048
  != wp_offset 248, len 248

The write plug rejects the out-of-order tail with BLK_STS_IOERR, causing
f2fs_stop_checkpoint() and remounting the filesystem read-only:

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: rtw88: usb: bound what the driver feeds the after-DTIM queue

Frames routed to the high queue are transmitted right after DTIM beacons
only, inside the ATIM window, while they wait in the shared TX page pool.
The driver puts no limit on how many it hands over, so as long as one
station dozes, any sustained broadcast or multicast traffic outruns the
drain and empties the pool: measured on an RTL8822BU AP with a single
client in power save and ~40 frames/s of mDNS chatter, the free page
count at 0x240 goes from 1803 to 16 in about 100 seconds and stays there
for as long as the traffic lasts. From that point every other transmit
queues behind the backlog, authentication responses arrive too late for
anyone to join, and the reserved page download fails ("error beacon
valid"). The AP keeps beaconing and only a reboot recovers.

Feed the high queue through a small budget that refills below the
measured drain rate (about 3 frames per DTIM, ~15/s at dtim_period 2 on
the default 2 TU ATIM window); whatever exceeds the budget leaves on its
access category queue right away. The high queue backlog is now bounded
by the burst size under any load, so the page pool cannot run dry, at
the price that a dozing station may miss part of a broadcast storm.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: rtw88: usb: route bmc frames via the high queue only for DTIM delivery

In AP mode every broadcast and multicast data frame is routed to
TX_DESC_QSEL_HIGH, the after-DTIM queue, whether or not anybody is
asleep. The firmware drains that queue at beacon pace, a dozen or so
frames per second measured on RTL8822BU, while one associated client's
mDNS/SSDP chatter alone exceeds that. The excess accumulates inside
the chip until the shared TX page pool is exhausted (measured: 14 of
1803 pages left). From that point every host-sourced frame queues
behind the backlog: authentication responses reach the air seconds
after the client has given up, so no station can associate anymore,
and the beacon reserved-page download fails the BCN_VALID poll
("error beacon valid") because it needs pages from the same pool. The
AP keeps beaconing, so the failure looks like a silent RX stall and
only a reboot recovers.

mac80211 already decides when after-DTIM delivery is needed: it sets
IEEE80211_TX_CTL_SEND_AFTER_DTIM on bmc frames only while at least one
station is actually dozing. Honor that instead of routing
unconditionally: flagged frames keep going through the high queue with
the MORE_DATA and HGQMD handling introduced by commit 076f786a0ae1
("wifi: rtw88: Fix AP mode incorrect DTIM behavior"), everything else
leaves at line rate through the AC queues. This partially reverts the
usb.c hunk of that commit, whose unconditional routing is what lets
the backlog build up.

On a bench AP (USB2, 20 MHz, WPA2, hostapd, a Windows client driven
through disconnect/reconnect cycles): reconnects fail 0/5 on RTL8822BU
and 0/3 on RTL8821CU before this change, and pass 10/10 and 5/5 with
it, with the page pool staying healthy and no beacon errors logged.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/shmem: honour F_SEAL_EXEC when an ACL is set

The owner of a memfd sealed with F_SEAL_EXEC can still change its
execute bits by setting a POSIX access ACL. With CONFIG_TMPFS_POSIX_ACL,
this lets an unprivileged owner make a non-executable memfd executable,
bypassing vm.memfd_noexec=2.

simple_set_acl() updates i_mode directly, bypassing the seal check in
shmem_setattr(). Add shmem_set_acl() to check the resulting mode. Share
the F_SEAL_EXEC check with shmem_setattr() using memfd_check_seals_mode()
in include/linux/memfd.h.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/userfaultfd: only allocate anon_vma in CoW mappings

find_vma_and_prepare_anon() can end up allocating an anon_vma in VMAs that
are not CoW mappings, which is wrong.

If we have a MAP_SHARED R/O file mapped, we lack VM_SHARED (but do have
VM_MAYSHARE) and lack VM_MAYWRITE.

While uffd later rejects such mappings (uffd registration requires
VM_MAYWRITE, see comment in validate_dst_vma) find_vma_and_prepare_anon()
still wrongly allocates an anon vma before it validates the vma.

This in turn later confuses copy_page_range()->vma_needs_copy() such
that we end up calling copy_hugetlb_page_range() with ranges that
actually do not contain *any* per-pagetable information that would
require copying, which is the basis for PMD-table sharing in the first
place.

copy_hugetlb_page_range() should not have to worry about shared
PMD tables at all: it doesn't make any sense to copy page tables that are
shared, as they can be fully recreated later. Ending up in the function
with shareable page tables is the real issue.

If a destination PMD table is shared in copy_hugetlb_page_range(), it
might get concurrently unshared as we are not holding relevant
locks, resulting in us using a page table that is no longer mapped and
possibly freed after calling:

	dst_pte = huge_pte_alloc(dst, dst_vma, addr, sz);

To fix it, do not allocate an anon_vma in non-CoW mappings and add a
safety guard to copy_hugetlb_page_range(), making sure that we never
end up messing with shared PMD tables in there.

Before commit 867a43a34ff8a ("userfaultfd: use per-vma locks in userfaultfd
operations") we would always validate the VMA before allocating an
anon_vma, and consequently never wrongly allocate an anon_vma.

As uffd_lock_vma() is part of the same lookup machinery and
also contains a misleading VM_SHARED check, change that one as well
directly for consistency.

A follow-up cleanup will stop taking the hugetlb_vma_lock_read(src_vma)
lock in copy_hugetlb_page_range() entirely. Further, the usage of
VM_SHARED in userfaultfd code should be cleaned up later to focus on
CoW vs. non-CoW mappings.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

platform/chrome: cros_usbpd_notify: Only use drvdata when parent is GOOG0004

cros_usbpd_notify_probe_acpi() takes the EC device pointer from
dev_get_drvdata(dev->parent) and assumes it is a struct cros_ec_device.
That only holds when GOOG0003 is a child of GOOG0004. On older devices
without that hierarchy, such as Google Nami, GOOG0003 and GOOG0004 are
siblings under the ACPI EC (PNP0C09):

  PNP0C09:00 (acpi-ec)
  |-- GOOG0003:00 (cros-usbpd-notify-acpi)
  `-- GOOG0004:00 (cros_ec_lpcs)

Before commit db65a06d10b3 ("ACPI: EC: Convert the driver to a platform
one") the parent platform device had no driver data, so the driver
warned and continued without an EC pointer, as intended for these
devices. Since that commit the ACPI EC driver stores its struct acpi_ec
there, so the driver treats a struct acpi_ec as a struct cros_ec_device
and calls cros_ec_cmd() on it for every USB-C PD host event. Plugging
or unplugging a charger then intermittently oopses, followed by soft
lockups and a hung system:

  BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffffff9cf03220
  #PF: supervisor write access in kernel mode
  Hardware name: Google Nami/Nami, BIOS  09/19/2019
  Workqueue: kacpi_notify acpi_os_execute_deferred
  RIP: 0010:native_queued_spin_lock_slowpath+0x29d/0x330
  Call Trace:
   _raw_spin_lock_irqsave+0x59/0x80
   __mutex_lock.constprop.0+0x129/0x930
   cros_ec_cmd_xfer+0x2a/0xf0 [cros_ec_proto]
   cros_ec_cmd_xfer_status+0x1a/0x90 [cros_ec_proto]
   cros_ec_cmd+0xb7/0x140 [cros_ec_proto]
   cros_usbpd_get_event_and_notify+0x42/0xc0 [cros_usbpd_notify]
   acpi_ev_notify_dispatch+0x4e/0x70
   acpi_os_execute_deferred+0x1a/0x30

Only read the parent's driver data when the parent's ACPI node is
GOOG0004, and otherwise continue without an EC pointer. While at it,
drop the reference taken by fwnode_get_parent().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: re-point retained control chunks on association migration

sctp_sock_migrate() transfers DATA chunk ownership but leaves retained
control chunks pointing at the old socket. A later retransmission can
therefore access the socket after it has been freed.

Extend the migration walk to cover retained control chunks and use
sctp_control_set_owner_w() to assign their new owner. Reuse the DATA
ownership check so each chunk is processed once per pass, even when it
is reachable through multiple lists or retained pointers.

Preserve a control chunk's existing authentication key across migration
so its final release can still generate SCTP_AUTH_FREE_KEY when needed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: hold shkey across socket migration

sctp_sock_migrate() transfers queued DATA skbs from the old socket to the
new one. skb_orphan() invokes sctp_wfree() during that transfer and drops
the skb-owned shared-key reference.

If userspace has removed that key from the association, this can be the
final reference. The following sctp_set_owner_w() then dereferences the
freed chunk->shkey while trying to take the new owner reference.

Take a temporary shared-key reference before orphaning the skb and release
it after the new owner has taken its reference. This preserves the selected
authentication key throughout the ownership transfer.

Bug found and triaged by OpenAI Security Research and
validated by Trail of Bits.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: arm64: Use kvm_s2_fault_vma_info in gmem_abort()

gmem_abort() maps at s2fd->fault_ipa, which HPFAR_EL2 holds at 4K
granularity whatever the page size. The generic page-table code aligns
it, but pkvm_pgtable_stage2_map() looks up existing mappings over
[addr, addr + size), so on a pKVM host with pages larger than 4K a
guest_memfd-backed guest that faults past the first 4K of a page can
find its neighbour's mapping, get -EAGAIN and take the same fault
forever.

The memory fault exit reports s2fd->fault_ipa too, which for a nested
guest's fault is the nested IPA rather than the canonical one
kvm_gmem_get_pfn() failed on.

Take the addresses from kvm_s2_fault_vma_info instead, as
user_mem_abort() does, and report the canonical gfn in the memory fault
exit. kvm_s2_fault_get_vma_info() itself isn't called: a guest_memfd
memslot's userspace_addr doesn't need to be backed by a VMA.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iommu/arm-smmu-v3: Handle ARM erratum for CONT under invalidation with SVA

The erratum (MMU-700: #3777127, S3: #3673557) deals with under
invalidation of a CONT PTE grouping in the SMMU. The recommended work
around is to use a range invalidation that spans the entire CONT. The only
user of CONT in the kernel right now is through SVA sharing a CPU page
table that contains a CONT created by the mm.

Previously it was thought that this errata was dealt with because the
driver always uses range invalidation. However, there is a subtle detail
in the errata that the invalidation range must fully enclose the entire
CONT for it to work.

It seems that two sequential range invalidations, with a split point
falling inside a CONT grouping, will not prevent the errata.

The SMMU's range invalidation generation algorithm does not produce a
single invalidation for a single SVA invalidation request, nor does the mm
carefully align the SVA invalidation ranges to accommodate the splitting
of the invalidation into several ranges.

Thus, when processing a SVA invalidation, the range invalidation splitting
routine can generate a range invalidation that is split in the middle of
the CONT and risk under invalidation from this errata. This condition
could be triggered by a malicious userspace manipulating the TLB gathers
via mmap/mprotect/munmap.

Update the errata list to the include the S3 variation, detect the IOMMUs
that have it, and then have SVA invalidations use a simplified version of
the over invalidation algorithm from the tlbi rework series. This ensures
that a single range invalidation is issued for a single MMU notifier
callback and now the range invalidation is guarenteed to cover any posible
CONT.

Future work to add CONT to iommu_domain page tables should either use this
one-invalidate/one-range invalidation algorithm or disable CONT support in
the iommu_domain.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ata: libata-scsi: reject data-in commands with a data-out buffer

SG_IO can submit a data-in SCSI command with DMA_TO_DEVICE. The
scatterlist can then contain pages pinned without write access.
ata_scsi_rbuf_fill() writes simulated replies to that scatterlist;
in the reported case, the copy tried to write the shared zero page
and faulted in the kernel.

The same mismatch can affect SG_IO commands translated by libata.
ZBC IN and GET PHYSICAL ELEMENT STATUS completion handlers can modify
the receive buffer even if the drive aborts the command. For ATAPI,
the successful INQUIRY completion also rewrites the buffer in
atapi_fixup_inquiry().

Reject these mismatched commands before the buffer is written or the
command is issued. Report ABORTED COMMAND / DATA IN BUFFER ERROR because
the CDB itself can be valid; the supplied transfer direction is wrong.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

batman-adv: tt: only update flags for TT events

In the first implementation of the translation table events, it was only
possible to announce:

* ADD: new locally detected client
* DEL: disappeared local client

If an ADD event was queued and then a DEL event was queued in the same
timeslot, it is valid to destroy both events because nothing actually
changed for remode nodes

But with commit 3c4f7ab60cc2 ("batman-adv: improve the TT component to
support runtime flag changes") and subsequent changes, it could also happen
that there are extra ADD events:

* ADD: _NEW_ locally detected client
* ADD: already existing client with new flags
* DEL: disappeared local client

The first and the last type of event could in theory still be removed
together from the (to be announced) events queue. But if the "update flags"
ADD is dropped together with the DEL, it would still leave global
translation table of a remote node in the incorrect state - believing that
the client didn't disappear.

If a detected client was previously announced, a DEL event must only
overwrite the "update flags" ADD but the DEL itself must still continue to
exist in the (to be anounced) events queue. For now, adjustment of the
announced flags is used for everything instead of dropping already queued
up events completely.

Similarly, a DEL followed by an ADD caused both entries to be deleted. But
the new ADD could announce flags changes which were not yet present for the
client before it was marked for DELetion. The new ADD must therefore only
overwrite the DEL - but still be kept.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

batman-adv: tt: clear ROAM flag when re-adding a pending local client

When a ROAMING_ADV is received for an announced local client,
batadv_tt_local_mark_removed() sets BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM, queues a
DEL|ROAM change and marks the entry as BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING. If the
client sends a frame again before the next TTVN commit,
batadv_tt_local_add_existing() only clears the PENDING flag and returns
early. The ADD cancels the queued DEL, but the entry keeps the ROAM flag:

* batadv_is_my_client() reports the client as not served by this node
* batadv_tt_local_client_is_roaming() reroutes unicast frames for it to
  the node which sent the ROAMING_ADV

The ROAM flag is only removed with the next frame of the client.

Since BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM is set together with BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING,
it has to be cleared also at the same time with BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING
when the client roamed back.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ceph: clamp the inline data length in ceph_fill_inline_data()

The MDS decides how much inline data to attach to a reply, and the
client parses inline_len without any upper bound: ceph_decode_need()
only verifies that the message actually carries that many bytes.
ceph_fill_inline_data() then copies the data into a single folio
with no length check, so a malicious or buggy MDS returning more
inline data than the folio can hold writes past its end.

Clamp the length to folio_size() so both callers, handle_cap_grant()
and fill_inode(), are covered.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iommu/amd: Force device table to maximum size

IOMMU can perform out-of-bounds read of the device table entry (DTE)
that is adjacent to the last DTE and falls outside the device table.
For example, if the device table can hold 0 to N-1 entries, then the
IOMMU can be made to fetch the Nth entry, which falls outside the
device table.

The device table is owned by the hypervisor (HV) and is assigned in 4KB
pages that are contiguous in system physical address (SPA). If the
out-of-bound DTE falls on a guest-owned page, then the guest can exploit
this bug to setup malicious table walks to corrupt HV pages and/or bring
down the system. Note that this bug does not manifest when the device
table size is set to its maximum size of 2MB.

Therefore, force the device table size to the maximum 2MB on affected
processors. These are CPU family 0x17 (Zen1/Zen2) through family 0x1a
(Zen5/BRH).

This is a mitigation for CVE-2024-21963.

kdump reuses the previous kernel's device table only when the size
encoded in the IOMMU device-table register matches
pci_seg->dev_table_size. A mixed rollout disagrees: the unpatched
kernel uses the IVRS-derived size and the patched kernel uses 2MB,
so __reuse_device_table() rejects the table. On SNP-capable IOMMUs
that rejection panics the kdump kernel. Kernels that both have this
patch agree on 2MB and reuse succeeds. Update the production kernel
and the crash kernel together.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

x86/mm: Fix global ASID handed out to two processes

On AMD CPUs with INVLPGB, two live processes can get the same MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE
global ASID value. The two then hit each other's TLB entries, so each can read
or corrupt the other's memory.

The global ASID space is managed lazily. When a global ASID is freed, its bit is
set in the global_asid_freed bitmap. Once the free ASID search reaches the end
of the global_asid_used bitmap, a global flush is done to really reclaim the
lazily freed global ASIDs.

However, the current code can assign the same global ASID to two different
processes, if one process is assigned MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE - 1, another process
MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE, and both stick around (keeping their global ASID numbers in
use) until the search wraps around again.  At that point a third process could
also get assigned MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE.

    the highest ASID stays in use, so it is not handed out again
      last_global_asid stays below it, so no reset
        the clear bits run out
          find_next_zero_bit() returns MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE
            global_asid_available > 0, so the failure is not caught
              MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE is handed out as an ASID

A search only looks at the bits below MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE, so it cannot see that
this value is in use. The next failed search hands it out again, even if the
first process still holds it.

The fix used here is to reset the global ASID space after a failed search, and
to search again. If that search fails too, no global ASID is handed out.

The test for !global_asid_available is removed, because use_global_asid() only
calls allocate_global_asid() if global_asid_available > 0. The remaining test is
for a condition that should be impossible.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

arm64: sdei: Preserve the interrupted context's exception registers

An SDEI event is dispatched by firmware regardless of PSTATE.DAIF, so it
can interrupt the kernel where the exception registers are live:

 - exception entry, before kernel_entry has saved ELR_EL1/SPSR_EL1 and
   before the C handler has read ESR_EL1/FAR_EL1;
 - exception return, after kernel_exit has loaded ELR_EL1/SPSR_EL1 and
   before the ERET.

An IRQ or pseudo-NMI cannot arrive there with PSTATE.I set. Firmware
saves only x0-x17, PC and PSTATE around an SDEI event, so a synchronous
exception taken by the handler overwrites the interrupted context's
ELR, SPSR, ESR and FAR. do_sdei_event() only notices that ELR changed,
and warns.

The interrupted context then carries on with the handler's state. A
task interrupted on its way into the kernel can be sent SIGILL for the
handler's kernel data abort. A task interrupted on its way back to user
space ERETs to EL1, at the handler's fixup address, with user registers
loaded.

With SDEI delivering NMI backtraces, this happens in normal operation.
The handler runs show_regs(), which reads through possibly-NULL pointers
with the _nofault() accessors. print_worker_info() faults this way for a
kworker that is not running a work item, and a single sysrq-l warned
once per such kworker.

Save ELR, SPSR, ESR and FAR in __sdei_handler() before
irqentry_nmi_enter(), which can take an exception too, and restore them
after irqentry_nmi_exit().

Once they are restored, a nested exception is harmless if its handler is
safe in NMI context. That holds for EL1 data aborts on translation,
permission and access-flag faults, which never take the mmap lock in NMI
context, and for BRK. Warn once, with the syndrome, about any other
exception class.
